speechtext: The House resumed from Tuesday, January 22, consideration of the motion of Mr. Stevens that Bill C-15, an Act respecting investment in Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Regional Development; and on the amendment of Mr. Gray (Windsor West) (p. 1302).

Mr. Speaker, when I left off my participation in this debate two days ago, I had suggested that what we should be doing instead of opening our doors through Investment Canada is finding a new mechanism to ensure that investment money, whether Canadian based or from countries beyond our borders, can be used to the benefit of Canada and its people. In my remaining five minutes, I want to indicate how I see those funds being attracted to the investment needs of Canada.
One of the things we should be looking at is a greater intensity in trying to match the need. When I talk about the need, I mean people who have ideas, entrepreneurs who need capital to develop their ideas into fruitful enterprises which will create real jobs and therefore wealth. On the other hand, we have people in Canada who do have money and who want to invest in new enterprises to create additional wealth for themselves while at the same time setting up a new business that in itself will create wealth for the participants. We would be better off if Investment Canada were to become the vehicle to match investors with needs. Perhaps from time to time there will be no investors in Canada prepared to take the risk to develop new enterprises. Perhaps at times there will be ideas generated in other countries. Perhaps the originators of those ideas may want to bring them to Canada to assist us. We are not opposed to that. We want to make sure that whatever mechanism we establish will be for the benefit of Canadians.
We should also ensure that our mechanisms prevent the outright takeover of Canadian-based, Canadian-owned companies by foreign interests. That is not in the best interests of this country or its people. For example, if you have a functioning plant whose owner wants to retire and dispose of his assets, I
think the Government of Canada has a responsibility to ensure every step is taken and every avenue explored to find a Canadian buyer. When it comes to looking for employees, the Government does not hesitate to say to an individual who wants to bring someone from abroad to work in his or her facility, whether a small or a large business, "Have you done a job search in Canada? Have you gone through Canada Manpower? And have you searched across the nation to find an out-of-work Canadian to fill this position?" Very clearly this was a policy of the old government and it is a policy of this Government. Why do we not use the same philosophy when it comes to investment? It is capital that is not working. It is unemployed capital that we are trying to put to use. As a Government and as a Parliament, we should be saying to people who have need for investment: "Have you fully searched throughout Canada? Here are some things we can do to help match you with an individual who has some out-ofwork capital".
We would be much better off, Mr. Speaker, if we took that approach rather than saying that the doors are open, buy us out. I do not want to be bought out. I want Canadians to have full partnership in this country. I think the Government has a responsibility to ensure that people have every opportunity and it should assist and boost them along.
I am quite pleased to see the motion before us to delay this Bill so that the Government can have the six months it needs to rethink its rhetoric and to put in place something that is practical for our country.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to take part in the debate today, and I would like to ask the Government to consider our proposal to postpone adoption of this legislation for six months as an opportunity to reconsider and rethink this Bill.
It is clear that basically, the Government tabled this legislation on investment in Canada for the purpose of facilitating the entry into this country of investments that will create jobs. However, I feel that the Progressive Conservative Government made a very serious mistake in attempting to rewrite the history of the Foreign Investment Review Agency.
Naturally, a new Government will think it can do better than its predecessor and want to start from scratch and rewrite history. Nevertheless, the Minister should consider how the Foreign Investment Review Act has benefitted Canada. Granted, a number of administrative adjustments to the legislation

January 24, 1985
Investment Canada Act
were made in the course of its history. From time to time, the Agency was criticized for taking too long to respond to applications by prospective buyers of Canadian companies or prospective investors. However, it was a matter of administrative measures that could easily be dealt with, but to repeal the existing legislation which protects our Canadian economic interests, which is what the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion wants to do, is, I think, a very serious mistake. The Government's Bill will neither boost the economy nor create the expected jobs. And why will the Bill fail to live up to the Government's expectations? Because it gives foreign investors carte blanche. In fact, it allows them to come and buy whatever they want in Canada, with no consideration for the country's economic interests.
Over the years we have had regional development policies enabling the Government, whenever appropriate, to attract investment to a region with less industrial development and higher unemployment than other regions. Mr. Speaker, I maintain that this regional development policy has been beneficial to our country. I also believe that letting foreign investors invest only where they want to put their money and, as often happens, purchase a Canadian company with which they compete on the international market, will, in the long term, have a disastrous effect on the Canadian economy, despite the short-term financial gain. We already have a very high concentration of Canadian companies. Competition in Canada is already limited as it is. It is a fact that in many sectors of the economy, the market is dominated by only one or two companies, and this lack of free competition is not always to the advantage of the consumer. In fact, if the Canadian economy were more competitive, we would all be better off.
The policy this Government is proposing will be a blow to the free market system in Canada. I predict that foreign investors are going to buy Canadian companies to reduce competition on the Canadian market and that both in the short and long run, this will not be in the best interests of Canadians or of Canada's economy.
I think it is incredible that the new Government is getting involved in decontrol of investment in our country. This does not happen in any other industrialized country, and especially not in those countries that compete with us on the international market.
Mr. Speaker, just try and buy a Japanese company or a French company, just try to invest in countries that are our main competitors, in Japan and in the Common Market countries, and let me know whether they let you invest freely, without any constraints, and without making any commitment to promote the economic interests of the country concerned. It just does not happen! It doesn't happen in France, it doesn't happen in Germany, and it doesn't happen in Japan. And why should we let it happen in Canada? Because the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion wants to do some Americans a
favor. Some of those big American corporations felt frustrated in the past because they could not take over certain Canadian companies and that was because at the time, we judged that the take-overs would not be in the best interests of this country.
I think it is very sad that one of the first actions of this new Government should be to bow to certain American economic interests. To do a few Americans a favour, we are risking our economic stability and our ability to compete freely on the Canadian market. I also predict that this kind of legislation will not create those hoped-for jobs.
I am particularly concerned about this offer the Minister made together with the introduction of his bill to sell a number of major Crown corporations which have played, are playing and should continue, in my view, to play an important economic role in this country. I am referring to such corporations as Canadair, from Montreal, and de Havilland, from Toronto, which are operating in a high technological industry with great job creating potential in Canada, and which the government might be tempted to sell off at bargain prices to foreign interests which will not protect the permanent job security given to many workers with these two aeronautics industries in the Montreal and Toronto areas.
For these reasons, we will fight against this bill as long as the government will not commit itself to imposing specific conditions on those who want to invest in Canada, in order to create jobs and protect existing ones in our country, so that the firms which might be sold to foreign interests may continue to operate and play a significant economic role in Canada. I suggest that the House should not adopt this bill, for it is much too dangerous.

Mr. Speaker, I too want to say a few words on Bill C-15 and argue in the House that we should be delaying this Bill for several months until the Government has a chance to reassess it once again.
There is a myth in this country that foreign ownership of our industries has made Canada a very prosperous country. I would like to make the argument that that is not the case. So much foreign ownership of our key resources has made us a poorer country and over the years has lost us many thousands of jobs.

In this country, Mr. Speaker, 26 per cent of our industries are controlled by foreigners, compared with 3 per cent in France and the United States, and only 1 per cent in Japan. [English]
The contrast is really quite stark in terms of our country and their countries with regard to foreign ownership of our economy. If you look at it sector by sector, in 1980, 1981 and 1982 some 48 per cent of our manufacturing in Canada was foreign
January 24, 1985

owned. Some 76 per cent of our rubber industry was foreign owned. In 1982, 19 of the 50 largest firms in this country were foreign controlled.
I think there are a number of consequences of foreign ownership for our economy that make this country much poorer than it could be when compared to other industrialized nations around the world. One of the consequences of foreign ownership is that our industrialized base becomes very fragmented because our economy tends to be a mini-version of the economy of the United States. It tends to mirror that of the United States. The United States has a much larger market than Canada. Its market is 10 times the size of Canada's. For example, if the United States has 10 firms in a particular industry, such as refrigeration, we in this country, because we are a mini-version of the United States, tend to have the same 10 firms in that same industry. We simply do not have the market to support that kind of industrial breakdown. Therefore, we have more unemployment and less efficiency than in the United States because of the varied sizes of our markets.
Even many efficient firms in Canada tend to close down because of decisions that are made in foreign boardrooms, particularly in the United States of America. I recall very vividly that a couple of years ago the Bowater plant in Newfoundland laid off some 700 employees despite the fact that it was making profits and paying dividends to its shareholders. In fact, it laid off 700 employees at a time when it paid some $40 million worth of dividends to foreign shareholders in the previous two years from 1980 to 1982. An efficient firm will also close down in this country because it is part of a multinational corporation if it is not in the interests of the corporation as a whole to keep that firm in operation in this country. This can happen because of plans made elsewhere in the world or in the United States of America. We have seen this happen time and time again.
When looking at industrial development in Canada, one sees that often the most efficient, stable or successful industries are those that are Canadian owned and not excessively fragmented. Examples of this can be seen in the steel industry, the breweries and the telecommunications industry, to name but a few.
Another consequence of foreign ownership in Canada that makes us poorer is that we tend to lose out on an awful lot of research and development. Members of the Conservative Party, when they were in opposition and during the election campaign, said: "Elect us and we will increase that percentage of money that goes into research and development". Yet we heard the mini-budget statement in November in which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) cut back again on many research programs and particularly on funding for the National Research Council of Canada. Once again we are seeing a breach of a very important election promise and a breach of faith and understanding of the Canadian people about future industrialized development.
Investment Canada Act
As I said, in 1981 we spent 1.2 per cent of our GNP on research and development. The United States spent 2.5 per cent of its GNP on research and development and Japan spent 2 per cent of its GNP on research and development. France spent 1.8 per cent of its GNP on research and development. As you can see, Mr. Speaker, we are behind almost every industrialized country in the world in terms of money that is spent on research and development. Our percentage of GNP spent on research and development is lower than many other countries such as Belgium, Norway and Yugoslavia. It is my understanding that we are on a par with countries such as Ireland and Egypt when it comes to money being spent on research and development.
Looking at the new and innovative fields of high technology, Canada is now importing around twice as much high technology as it exports. That of course means a loss of jobs for Canadians and particularly for young people. In 1980 our high-technology trade deficit was some $8 billion. In computer technology alone the estimates are that by the year 1990, only five years away, our trade deficit could hit some $10 billion. I do not see any reason in the world why we should have a trade deficit of some $10 billion in computer technology when we are moving into an era in which every child will have a computer on every desk in every classroom in our country. There is no reason at all why we cannot be producing those computers here at home, whether in Quebec, Ontario, the West or the Atlantic Provinces. There is no reason why we cannot be supplying our schools and hospitals with our own computers. There is no reason why we should not be supplying not only the government sector with our own computers but the private sector as well. If we had some imagination, that is the way it would go. One of the consequences of foreign ownership is that we do not do the research and development and forward planning we need because it is done for us in Dallas, Texas, New York, or any place which seats the headquarters of the firm.
Another consequence of foreign ownership is that there are often exports in Canada which are restricted because the parent companies make decisions about export policies in their branch plants around the world. If we look at the Gray report which came out ten or 12 years ago, it indicates that about 58 per cent of Canada's manufacturing subsidiaries operated under some kind of export restriction. It was over 50 per cent then, and the situation is almost as bad today.
In 1981 Statistics Canada provided a report which was quite controversial in Canada. The report indicated that foreign-owned firms imported about four times as much as domestic firms in the same field. That meant the loss of thousands of jobs for Canadians. Therefore, a foreign firm, because it is a subsidiary of a company which is based elsewhere, will tend to import four times as much as a Canadian firm. In addition, foreign ownership has made us a supplier of raw materials and an importer of manufactured goods. The deficit in manufacturing in 1981 alone was some $21 billion. That resulted in the

Investment Canada Act
loss of thousands and thousands of jobs in Canada each and every year.
We must also consider the outflow of capital in terms of dividends, interest payments and direct capital which amounts to billions of dollars. Between 1976 and 1981 it amounted to an outflow of some $38 billion of Canadian capital by foreign shareholders in terms of dividends, interest rates and direct profits to countries other than Canada.
These are but a few of the arguments which lead me to support the motion which is before the House and to call upon the Government to rethink the whole foreign investment strategy. The agency which is being replaced is FIRA. FIRA had most of its teeth pulled by the former Liberal Government. The former Government and this Government have been backing away, and I believe for the wrong kinds of reasons. I would argue before the House that the Government should accept the amendment, do some rethinking, and come up with a stronger Bill which will help Canadians take control of their own destiny and economy and build a society which is controlled by Canadians. If we do that we can start in the 1990s and the latter part of the 1980s to repatriate the Canadian economy, just as we did with the Constitution in 1982. If we do that, we are making some meaningful progress in terms of making Canada a country in which Canadians control their own destiny, a country which will have jobs for every Canadian, regardless of where they may live. However, we will not achieve that by trying to woo large multi-national corporations which will come into the country, set up subsidiaries, do little research and development, import components and parts from abroad, export little and create few jobs for Canadians. Foreign companies often set up in communities such as mining towns which become single-industry communities. When it is no longer possible to be in that community, they leave, destroying a town such as Schefferville in Quebec. It destroys the future for the people who live in those communities.
In closing, I would like to say that I come from the Province of Saskatchewan, which probably has more locally-owned and locally-controlled industries and businesses than any other province in Canada. That is a result of the tremendous power of the co-operative movement. The wheat pools which are owned by the farmers now sell 70 per cent of our wheat. Saskatchewan has a powerful credit union movement. There are credit unions in every town and village across the province. Saskatchewan has co-op stores, retail stores and all the businesses in which they are involved, such as the refining of petroleum. Saskatchewan also has a very powerful public sector, such as the Potash Corporation of Saskatchewan, the gas and oil companies and the Saskatchewan Power Corporation. I believe that all of these developments have contributed to the fact that our province has one of the two lowest unemployment rates in Canada. If we had followed that kind of a lead, this country would be better for each and every one of us.

Mr. Speaker, it is with a sense of history that one joins in the debate on Bill C-15. Indeed, Sir, this is part of an ancient debate which goes back to the time of Confederation and, in all probability, before that. When we talk about the movement of goods and capital between Canada and other countries, mainly the United States of America, there has always been a certain amount of discomfort on the part of Canadians because our neighbours to the south are so large in comparison to ourselves. We have never really known how to deal with this problem. When times have been good in Canada, we sometimes felt that we did not need the money coming across the border and legislation was passed, such as FIRA, which tried to keep it out. On the other hand, when times are not quite as good and we need more jobs in Canada, the tendency, as it is today, is to open up the doors, get rid of things like FIRA and invite some of that money into the country. I suspect, Sir, that this debate will continue to wax and wane over the next centuries as it has over the last.
What we see with Bill C-15 in comparison with the old FIRA is a difference in outlook towards life on the part of the Liberals and the socialists, on the one side, and the Conservatives on the other. If we examine what has been said during this debate by the Liberals and the New Democratic Party, we see that their view of life is very introspective. They tend to look inwards all the time. When there is any new development of any kind, their natural reaction is to be frightened. They tend to be reactionary. In their policies, they always tend to stress protection. They want to protect themselves from anything which might be happening. It seems, Sir, that the Liberals and the socialists are like so many snails. Whenever anything happens which comes close to them, they retreat back into their shells.
If we contrast this with the general views and principles espoused by the governing Party-which, I might add, represents the majority of Canadians who saw fit to elect this new Government with these new ideas with one of the largest majorities in Canadian history-we see that its views tend to be outward looking. We see opportunities and not threats when there are new developments in the world at large. We on this side of the House feel that Canadians can compete with anyone from any other country in the world. We have confidence in Canadians and in Canada.
In keeping with our views on the minimization of state interference and control in the lives of private citizens, what they can do with their own property, to whom they can sell, and so on, the legislation before us today was brought about. In Canada in the past we have tended to build walls around ourselves which have been so thick and so high that we ended up not being able to see over the top. We want to dismantle some of these walls and Bill C-15 is one of the ways in which we want to do that.
There is a new world out there. It is a new and exciting world and it is full of opportunities and challenge for Canadians. We feel that Canadians are up to that challenge and can
January 24, 1985

take advantage of it. My plea, Sir, isthat Canada gets plugged into the new world.
It is a simple fact, Mr. Speaker, that if we want a high standard of living in Canada-and that translates for most people into high wages-then we need capital investment in this country. If we want to be able to pay higher wages, it means that we have to have more machinery available to us so we can be more productive and that with the time which is put in by way of labour, we can extract more out and, as a consequence, can enjoy that higher standard of living. That means that capital investments are of the utmost importance to Canada and Canadians.
Under the previous administration in this country, although there was capital coming into Canada helping us develop our industries here, by the time that administration's stint was over and it had been thrown out by Canadians, that capital flow had reversed. Not only had that administration installed barriers to foreign capital coming into Canada, but it had also made it very difficult for Canadians to invest in their own country and Canadians were taking their capital abroad to the United States and other countries. Therefore, there was a net capital outflow from Canada, and that is one of the reasons we are saddled with so much unemployment today. It is a direct result of government policies in the past which have created this negative flow.
What we intend to do now and in the next few short years is to reverse that process so that we have a positive flow, so that Canadians will invest in their own country, because opportunities for profit making are here. We also must have money from abroad coming into Canada because we do not have enough in this country to provide all the jobs which we would like to see created in order to get the unemployment rate down. As a consequence of the reversal in capital flow, there will definitely be more employment. The horrendous figures for unemployment will get better and better as the years go by under the new Government and as this reversal is made possible. There will be increased business opportunities for Canadians whatever their line of business.
The principles contained in this Bill were expounded at length during the recent election campaign. They were a fundamental plank in the platform of the Progressive Conservative Party going into the election. These ideas received the overwhelming support of Canadians and, therefore, in my opinion it would be wise for the Opposition not to try to drag out debate for ever and ever by bringing in things like the six-month hoist which we are debating today, but rather accept the wishes of Canadians and help us constructively to make a better Bill. The Opposition should not object to the principle of the Bill and what Canadians want but should try to refine it and make it better. That, Sir, is my suggestion to opposition Members and I hope they will take heed of it.

Mr. Speaker, I would ask the Government to reconsider the Bill it calls Investment Canada. I think it should be called the foreign investment act because it does absolutely nothing for invest-
Investment Canada Act
ment in this country. The only beneficiaries of this Bill will be foreign investors.
If the Government would only take the time to look at this Bill, it would see the fallacies which are contained within it. How can we expect a foreign company which owns a branch plant in Canada to maintain the research and development which is maintained by a Canadian-owned company? It is just not going to happen. The parent company in a country other than Canada, primarily the United States, is not going to let it happen. The politics of that country are not going to let it happen. How can branch plants export products the way Canadian-owned companies can? It just is not possible. It is not allowed by the parent company. Only a Canadian-owned company which has developed the product with state of the art technology can export it. A Canadian branch plant is just that, a store-front to sell an existing product in Canada. It is nothing more and will be nothing more. How can the Government say it is going to create more jobs with this Investment Canada Act? A branch plant is forced by its very nature to import more parts and equipment and technology than a Canadian-owned company would. Both statistics and common-sense tell us that, Mr. Speaker.
When there is a downturn in the economy, where will the jobs be lost? They will be lost faster and in greater numbers among foreign-owned companies because they will protect the operation in the country of origin. They are not going to be concerned about branch plants in Canada or unemployed Canadians. Canadians will be employed if the work is there but when a downturn comes, when difficult times arrive, it will be primarily Canadians who suffer and they will suffer first.
That is not to say this Party is against foreign investment; not at all. Foreign investment is extremely important. It has played a great role in the economy of this country. We invest in foreign countries as well so it would be extremely shortsighted to say we should not allow foreign investment in this country. However, that is not the question. The question is, if we completely destroy the existing framework which allows us to monitor and regulate foreign investment in this country, which gives us a window on our economy and our industries, we will be courting disaster. We will suffer economic reversals the like of which we have never suffered before.
You can say that FIRA has not worked. Certainly the Government says FIRA is too restrictive. My friend from Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) says that FIRA was not strict enough. Obviously the former Liberal Government was doing something right. So why not take this Act, as my colleague from Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) has said, and adjust it and see where the problems are? Certainly there were problems with FIRA. Application review took far too long and that is just one problem; but here we are dismantling a positive Act and agency which served this country and its economy very well.
The Government has said this Bill will be a boon for the economy. The Americans in turn have said they are not

January 24, 1985
Investment Canada Act
waiting at the Canadian border with bags of money. Do not expect a change in FIRA to bring American investors pouring into the country. The Americans are saying that they are not going to pour into this country and invest in great numbers, yet this is what the Government is basing its whole argument upon. It is willing to destroy completely the economic fabric of this country in order to take a flying chance that there will be additional investment in Canada. We need jobs now and if we cannot get them, for heaven's sake, let us be prepared to do everything we can to retain the jobs we have.
The Government has encouraged foreign investment in Canada. It wants that investment. The question is, what will happen with this framework? Any direct takeover worth less than $5 million will not be reveiwed under this Act. I say to the Government that nothing is going to be reviewed under this Act. You cannot tell me that, given the dialogue the Government has started in order to encourage this friendly attitude towards the U.S., it will now suddenly review the activities and investments of Americans in Canada. No, it is not going to do that. It was a fallacy to imagine that was going to happen.
This is particularly evident in the energy sector where the most damage is going to occur. Stock prices in the energy industry are depressed. There are multinationals who perhaps have the marketing capacity right now but they do not have the resource capacity and Canadian energy companies are ripe for takeover by foreign firms. The Government is going to turn a blind eye into this danger, yet the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) has said that enhanced Canadian participation is one of the objectives of her Government. There is obviously a very large discrepancy in the policies advocated by two different Ministers of this Government.
A lot of the complaints about FIRA have naturally come from those people who are going to do business with the companies investing in Canada, such as lawyers and accountants. That is natural. But it is not the responsibility of those people to look after the economy of this country. The Government has to do that and the Government is sadly neglecting or completely abandoning its role. What will happen to small business? The Americans are not going to invest in new businesses, they are primarily going to take over existing Canadian businesses and this is where we will lose the jobs. What about the Government's promise to free up capital for small businesses and Canadian businesses in general? Instead, it is leaping into the path of least resistance and doing something which does not require and has not been given any thought. Canadians have paid for the Canadianization of the energy sector but the Government is turning the clock back to the beginning and giving over the energy sector and other sectors of the economy to foreign investment. It will be all completely done away with in a few short years.
The Government has fostered the belief that foreign investment will mean investment will occur all over the country. The have-not areas will have their big moment and foreign companies are just going to come pouring into their regions. Well, that is not true; it is not going to happen. Statistics indicate
that if you lift the restraints on foreign investment, the foreign investors will all end up in the same area. They are like fast food outlets; they want to be on top of one another. How is this going to help one of the crying needs of this country, the need for regional development? Not only will it not help, it will exacerbate the problem and make it worse.
I think this is a travesty. The Government is not managing the economy, it is throwing it open helter-skelter and allowing foreign firms to come in and do whatever they want without regard to the Canadian economy itself. There is no consideration given to regional development or to where the economy is going and how jobs will be created. The Government is not prepared to give any thought to this. It only wishes to make friends on the other side of the border and it is doing so at the expense of the average Canadian. It is a travesty and I ask the Government to reconsider its position in this regard. It will be a very bad mistake if the Bill goes through in its present form.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to speak on Bill C-15 which proposes an agency called Investment Canada. Its purpose is to encourage investment in Canada by Canadians and non-Canadians.
The goals of this legislation have been set out as follows: one, to increase the entrepreneurial spirit in Canada; two, to increase research and development and the diffusion of new technologies; third, to expand Canada's economic and industrial base; four, to stimulate trade; and finally, to create jobs.
These goals I am sure are unexceptionable to all Members. Indeed, few Bills are introduced in the House to achieve more desirable goals than these. However, in measuring the value of this legislation surely we must examine whether the vehicle that it proposes is commensurate with the goals being sought, whether it reflects ideology or reality. I believe it reflects ideology, for the facts do not support the assumption that unencumbered foreign investment will achieve the economic benefits described.
Obviously, the biggest foreign investors are the Americans. To oppose this legislation is likely to evoke the usual allegations of anti-Americanism. Let me put that to rest. I am from Windsor and no Canadians are more familiar with Americans and less anti-American than we. Our jobs are unusually dependent upon the automobile industry, which is American owned and a classic example, through the auto pact, of what can be achieved through American or foreign investment when appropriate protections are implemented.
We are overwhelmed by the American print and broadcast media. We are Pistons fans, Lions fans, Tigers fans and Red Wings fans. Much of our entertainment and culture are pursued in Detroit. My wife and children are Americans. I obtained my doctorate in the United States.
We are not American but we do sometimes feel that our country has ceded us to the United States and that we must struggle against that, as we have with respect to the insensitive cuts applied to Windsor CBC. We struggle constantly to assert
January 24, 1985

our Canadian identity. We are then not only admirers of Americans, we are more aware than most Canadians of their shortcomings and the dangers of American dominance. We know that the pursuit of their national or corporate goals are unencumbered by philanthropy or concern about Canadian economic or political independence. We must pursue those goals ourselves. Where we have done so, Windsor has benefited.
On the other hand, hundreds of Windsor workers can testify to the results of the failure to defend Canadian interests. Let us just cite a few examples: the 200 jobs at Canadian Motor Lamp, the 500 jobs at Bendix, the 500 jobs at Dali Specialties and the 500 jobs at Walker Metals. They are jobs lost because Canada's interest was not sufficiently protected.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) went to New York to speak to the Economic Club and promised Americans that Canada would have a new direction and new national purpose. That purpose was to enhance Canada's sovereignty and independence by declaring that Canada was now open for unencumbered American investment. The Americans were ecstatic. They reap profits and payments amounting to 61 per cent of all external remittances. U.S. subsidiaries in Canada account for a large share of American exports to Canada. As was discovered by the U.S. Senate and the Harvard Business School, investment in Canada generates jobs in all sectors of the American economy. American professionals, technologists, scientists and engineers occupy the top spots in American-owned subsidiaries in Canada.
What benefits will Investment Canada bring? Let us look at the Government's goals. The first is to increase the entrepreneurial spirit. This, of course, must be one of the more curious aspects of the Bill. The Government says that the purpose is to increase Canadian investment. Of course, that should be done but nowhere in the Bill do we find any direction on how that should be achieved. We will disregard the philosophical nonsense involved in increasing Canadian entrepreneurial spirit by encouraging American investment and profit taking.
Will Bill C-15 increase research and development? This Bill is almost absurd in its disregard for reality. The fact of the matter is that the sorry record of Canadian industry in research and development is attributable largely to the failure of American subsidiaries because Canadian-owned industry has invested 10 per cent of sales as compared to the American Subsidiary rate of 3 per cent. That 10 per cent is quite comparable to a reasonable average.
We are supposed to gain technological diffusion. This is usually measured in terms of productivity but, as the Science Council has reported, American subsidiaries have a very sorry record compared to Canadian-owned firms with respect to productivity improvement. Of course, technological diffusion will not be attained if we do not have recipients, and we do not have the scientific and engineering underpinning to receive such diffusion.
We are supposed to be expanding the economic and industrial base. That would assume technological diffusion and
Investment Canada Act
would be based on increased international markets, which are not attained. It depends upon reinvestment, which does not occur. It depends on foreign-owned subsidiaries buying supplies in Canada, which they do not do. Let me cite an example of what happens even under protective instances. Chrysler vans that are made in Windsor are composed 70 per cent to 80 per cent of out-sourced parts.
We are told that our trade will be stimulated but the record shows that foreign companies are geared only to Canadian markets. Indeed, apart from exports to parent companies which account for 90 per cent of those exports from this country, subsidiaries may be restricted by their parent companies and indeed may be subject to the extraterritorial application of U.S. restrictions.
Will jobs be created? Let us examine the record. In 1982, 50 per cent of all jobs lost in Canada were lost among those American-owned companies constituting a portion of the 50 largest companies in this country.
In considering this legislation, it is difficult to see what has motivated it. It is alleged that there is a discouragement of American investment, but in fact between 95 per cent and 98 per cent of the applications have been approved in the last couple of years. Only 50 per cent have been required to meet any job conditions and 15 per cent have involved no new jobs or any new investment. In fact, the Conference Board has pointed out that only 11 per cent of foreign investors were at all deterred by FIRA.
It may well be that prompter, more efficient processing of applications would help, but clearly if we wish to achieve what the Conservatives say we must achieve to increase trade, jobs, research and development and to expand our industrial base, then it should be provided for, as it is not in this legislation. Instead, the Government is offering up the country for sale. It is a garage sale in which the house and children are thrown in for good measure.
The fact is that the wreckage of FIRA is unlikely to achieve anything. As a matter of fact, when consulted on the matter, American bankers have said that if there is new investment it will probably be a decade before it occurs and most of it will go into primary industry, which is of no help to us at all. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has promised us a new direction and a new sense of national purpose. That is what is needed, but it will not be achieved by looking to the United States or elsewhere. No nation has pursued a national vision in a foreign territory. We must look to ourselves, to Canadian interests and investment opportunities, if we are to achieve those goals which this Bill seeks to achieve.

Since this is my second opportunity to take part in this debate, I will limit my remarks to the Bill as it relates to the situation of women in Canada. The number of women in the labour force is greater than ever. In 1981, 51.6 per cent of it were women. The Dodge report indicates that 10 years from now, women will account for 65 per cent of the labour force. The ever-increasing participation of women has mainly been confined to the service area. According to the latest figures published by the Department of Labour in February 1984, 61 per cent of all service employees in 1981 were women.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-15 is a threat to women workers in Canada, because they are employed in the service and administrative areas, and as we know this means in our small-and medium-sized businesses.
When one looks closer into the role of women in small- and medium-sized businesses, one realizes to what extent these are dependent on women. This legislation, as has been said repeatedly, is a threat to the integrity of our small businesses. It is a threat to the integrity of women employment in that sector. Most women remain confined to the traditional employment ghettoes, such as cashier, secretarial, sales jobs in stores, and so on and so forth. And it is precisely those jobs that are directly threatened by the advent of microtechnology. If we add the negative consequences of the Investment Canada Act to the jobs that will be suppressed by high technology, we see that women once more will be the victims of bad Government policies.
Moreover, there is a significant salary differential as between men and women for similar work. It is a fact that employers look for women workers for more routine-like, less stimulating and, above all, low-salary jobs.
In 1980, average women's earnings amounted to 58 per cent of men's earnings. The average salary is $15,000 for women, as against $29,000 for men. In the 25 to 34 age group, a man with a Grade 9 education earns $15,696, while a woman with an M.A. or even a P.h.D. degree earns less. Her average earnings are $15,527.
Many families depend on the financial contribution of outside working wives for an adequate family income. In 1980, more than 49 per cent of wives with salaried jobs were married to men earning less than $20,000 a year. Those women therefore were providing their families with much needed extra income. Without their participation in the labour force, many families would be living below the poverty line.
A number of reports and studies often referred to in parliamentary debates shed a spectacular light on the scope of the problem. And as I said, technological changes are a serious threat to the areas of employment that are traditionally reserved to women, at a time when they enter the labour force in ever-increasing numbers.
During the election campaign, the three main political parties made many policy statements on the necessity of implementing training and retraining schemes for women as well as affirmative action programs. For example, the statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) on the status of women shows that he seemed willing to provide new opportunities for women, and I quote:
Nothing less than a retraining program of unprecedented generosity and ingenuity would be needed to face up to this new reality, when hundreds of thousands of women will suffer financially unless we make a national commitment to prevent such conditions.
I have closely scrutinized the measures taken by the government since it came into power on September 4, and I regret to say that all those fine words about women like many others were nothing but pious wishes.
Mr. Speaker, I am trying to show the part played by women in the Canadian economy. She is by far the mainstay of the economy. She is often compelled to accept menial jobs either because of family responsibilities or lack of opportunities. Some women who are heads of families have been forced to take two part-time jobs because they could not get job security.
When a working women is found in a small- or medium-size business, either she works with her husband or she is selfemployed. Mr. Speaker, I have been made aware by my constituency office of the problems and discrimination experienced by women workers in their working environment, and today I must plead on their behalf.
The problem of employment for women has been raised on various occasions over the years. A policy in this field has yet to be developed. Past experience has shown that when a company is in financial straits, women are the first to be dismissed and are reduced to accepting part-time jobs, which condemns them to poverty in their old age. It is well known that low wages result in a small pension.
If Bill C-15 were passed in its present form, I think it would jeopardize all small- and medium-size businesses, which are the backbone of the Canadian economy. Moreover, the Investment Canada Bill does not guarantee in the least a strong economy and, still worse, it provides nothing at all to safeguard jobs in Canada. Mr. Speaker, I therefore hope that we will take all the time required in committee to make the necessary amendment to this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I have just a few comments on this Bill. I have not had an opportunity to speak to this issue so far in the debate and I think it is an important debate. It is one to which more attention should be paid. In it we find articulated some of the serious differences that exist between the Government and the New Democratic Party, in particular with respect to how we view the Canadian economy and how we view the global economy.

I think I am being fair to the Government if I say that it regards the global economy and the investment decisions made by the international investment community as a series of neutral and independent decisions which we in Canada, particularly those in government, have to take into account as simple facts of life similar to the way in which we take the weather into account. Viewing as a simple fact of life that investment decisions are made according to certain criteria, the responsibility of government is then to create in Canada the context, or, as the Conservatives would call it, the investment climate, in which, given the rules of investment behaviour, investment will come to Canada and not go to other countries.
We have a different view of those kinds of decisions. To start with, we would like to see an international economic order in which those decisions are not made independently in the boardrooms of multi-national corporations, or global corporations, as they are more appropriately called in many instances. We would like to see an international economic order in which those decisions were accountable to the wellbeing of the global economy itself and the well-being of countries, not just the ones in which investments may or may not be made but other countries as well.
Of course, that brings into play the whole question of the North-South dialogue, et cetera, not in any charity-related way but in the way the Brandt Commission so well indicated- that the economic well-being of the North is related to the economic well-being of the South.
But I would like to return to the major point which I wanted to make concerning how we in the NDP regard investment decisions. We see the criteria by which these decisions are made not as something with which we simply have to live. In the name of the public interest, of the well-being of the Canadian economy and of common good, we would want to see, if we were in government, these investment decisions made in the interests of Canada. The interests of investors should not stand against and above the interests of the community, in this case the interests of the country. This is why in the past we supported and indeed initiated from this side of the House ideas such as the Foreign Investment Review Agency.
We were not happy with FIRA. We did not think it did its job as well as it could have. We did not think it was tough enough with respect to foreign investment. Despite the existence of FIRA, there were many cases where companies met its requirements but, after having been allowed to invest in Canada, behaved in a way contrary to what they said they would do, in ways contrary to the Canadian public interest.
This is an internally coherent measure on the part of the Government. It is not that the Government is contradicting itself. It has a view of investment with which this piece of legislation is quite consistent. Its view is that as a country we should simply capitulate to international realities, that we should simply capitulate to the world of international investors and say that we as a government are here for whatever those
Investment Canada Act
guys would like. "You do not want to invest unless we have the following climate and conditions-that is our job", says the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). He says that it is their job as the Government to create the conditions in which investors feel good so that they will invest.
That is not the way we see it. We see it as not only acting against the interests of the Canadian economy but as acting against the future of the global economy and against the possibility of having a new, just and sustainable economic order in which one country is not played off against the other, in which workers and farmers in one country are not played off against workers and farmers in another, in which people generally are not played off against each other by those who decide where money will and will not be invested. I am referring to those who sit there and say: "Well, Canada likes to have certain environmental laws, it has a labour movement with which we have to contend and various other things. Unless it softens up and creates the right climate, perhaps we will invest somewhere else".
By acceding to this kind of attitude on the part of the investment community, the Government of Canada is not only acting against the interests of Canada but against the possibility of finally creating some day a global economy in which that kind of blackmail cannot occur. There is no other word for it. That is why corporations are in business, either domestically when they play one province off against another or internationally when they play one country off against another.
In this Bill we have a classic opportunity to see what are the differences between the New Democratic Party and the Government. Although we were always very unhappy with the tokenism involved in FIRA with respect to the Liberals, we see this as a step backward on the part of the Progressive Conservative Government. It is trying to abandon altogether any pretence of ensuring that foreign investors act in the interests of Canada. At least in that respect we might be able to say that the Government is being more honest. It is not interested in pretension; it is interested in coming clean about the way in which it views the world. Our objection is that we do not think the world operates that way. We do not think that the international investment community is a sort of innocent, well-meaning group of people who are asking themselves how they can benefit the world or how they can distribute goods and services in the most equitable way. We just do not fall for that line. We know that when they meet they have global profit strategies and do a lot of thinking about how they can play one country off against the other. We know that any country which takes the kind of supine, acquiescent role which the Government is now advocating for Canada will live to regret it.
Unfortunately it is not just the Government which will live to regret it. If it were only the Government, it would be all right because at least the Government would have brought it upon itself. Unfortunately all Canadians will come to regret the decision being taken by the Government in the form of this legislation. That is the unfortunate part.
I have nothing else to say with respect to this particular piece of legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I consider it my duty to take part in the debate on Bill C-15 to create Investment Canada which, in my opinion, is a mistake that all Canadians will regret in the future.
If we look at the history of the Foreign Investment Review Agency, as many have done before me, we see that the Agency was created in 1974 and given the responsibility to apply certain criteria. One thing we have to remember is that the major purpose of this agency was to guarantee that any foreign investment would produce substantial benefits for Canada. This means benefits from every aspect, especially with regard to jobs and to prevent wealthy foreign investors from taking over some of our major industries and making them into subsidiaries of an American, British or Australian parent company which would eventually have meant fewer jobs in Canada than if the same industry had been Canadian owned. However, I believe that FIRA had a much loftier purpose, namely to canadianize our economy and make us proud to be Canadians. We often hear that it was because we were afraid of American investment. There might be some truth in this, Mr. Speaker, when we think of the enormous strength of the United States, a country with a population of over 225 million while we are just 26 million. We have to find means to assert our Canadian sovereignty and give us this pride which we lacked for many years, but which has emerged gradually because we are still a young country. I can give you examples of this pride: the Canadian flag is one. In passing, I can assure the House that our pride is still increasing because, just recently, the Canadian union of automobile workers severed its ties with the International union so that the Canadian workers and American workers would handle their business separately.
This is a sign of canadianization and it shows the will for sovereignty and the pride of belonging to Canada.
We could also refer to history. It would have been very easy to let the Americans through in 1814 at Chateauguay, but a small handful of Canadians rose up against that notion for the simple reason that they were proud to be in their own country.
I said earlier that we had to give ourselves the tools to fight against foreign invasion, and that the investments we must fear most are naturally those from the United States since the Americans are so powerful. What saddens me the most about this change, which is simply a cosmetic change for appearances' sake, is that the new Investment Canada agency excludes 90 per cent of small businesses, which are responsible for creating the most jobs in Canada.
We have to recall also that, for all practical purposes, FIRA rejected only 3 per cent of all applications submitted to it. This goes to show, Mr. Speaker, that this agency created in 1974 was there to apply what I would call criteria of pride and to help Canada to progress independently, both at the economic and political levels, because if ever we lose our economic independence, we would quickly become politically dependent.
These are the reasons why I wanted to make my humble contribution to this debate, in an effort to increase the awareness of the Government because, even though it promised changes during the election campaign, it was simply a promise to add its own seasonings to the great banquet it would offer the Canadian people. That was its right, of course. But with this change that is basically radical, especially in the area of foreign investment, I think that viewed from the long term we are making a mistake.
I submit that with the Foreign Investment Review Agency, established a few years back, Canadians gave themselves something to be proud of. I referred to the flag. I could have referred to the national anthem. I could have referred to a number of other things. Those are landmarks, markers we set up from time to time along the road to free Canada from any investment that could be harmful to our national, political and especially to our economic unity.
Such is the contribution I wanted to make, because it is my feeling that in view of the data and figures which I brought up earlier, we are opening wide the door to foreign investment, and, as a result, to a loss of our political identity following the loss of our economy. If we look at the reason why FIRA was created in 1974, we find it was to safeguard the future, the jobs, the economy and the youth of this country. This is something that cannot be over-emphasized.
Recently, my good friend from Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) brought up before this House a striking example indeed of why the Foreign Investment Review Agency was established, when he referred to the University of Ottawa bookstore. This bookstore, as I think the Hon. Member mentioned, is a very large employer. It was in the process of being taken over by

It is interesting to note that there was very little, if any, consultation with respect to Bill C-15. This is an extremely important piece of legislation with very serious ramifications from coast to coast in this country, yet in its wisdom the Government decided there would be very little if any, consultation. I understand there was no consultation with the provinces or with the various interest groups. They would have appreciated the opportunity to give their point of view with respect to Bill C-15. The Government promised that it would be an open, accessible and consultative Government. However, with this particular piece of legislation it decided not to go through the consultation process.
The other observation I would like to make is that this is the first major piece of legislation for the new Government. It is interesting to note the Government's priorities. One can assume that because it is its first major piece of legislation it is the Government's top priority at this point in time. It is strange that that should be its top priority when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is telling Canadians that the top priority is the economy and jobs. There are other more important pieces of legislation that should be coming forward.
In announcing Bill C-15, the Minister responsible for industry stated that this legislation heralds a new day for Canada. Indeed it heralds a new day but it is a sad new day for this country. By introducing this Bill, the Government is dashing any hope of having Canada ever gain control over its own economy. It is dashing any hope of our becoming masters in our own home. The lack of concern among Tories for Canadian independence and sovereignty, whether political or economic, should not come as a surprise.
The Tories have never quite been able to shake the master-slave mode of thinking. In the early years of this century, the Tories were determined to keep us bound to Britain. Arthur Meighen said "ready, aye ready" to Lloyd George during the Chanak crisis. Now we have "Branch-Plant Brian" saying

"ready, aye ready" to Ronald Reagan and the captains of U.S. industry.

It is hardly a coincidence that the Government should make the announcement of FIRA's demise on the eve of the Prime Minister's cap-in-hand speech to the Economic Club of New York. I am sure he will make the corporate boys at the Iron Ore Company misty-eyed with pride.
The Minister responsible for industry in announcing this legislation stated that Canada is open for business. As my Leader has indicated, this country has always been open for business. It has never been closed to business. We have always welcomed foreign investment. We want foreign investment, but we want it on our terms. As my Leader quite eloquently put it, this country is not for sale. Yet the Government has put the "for sale" sign on Canada. It is prepared to sell out our cultural identity and our economic sovereignty.
The Minister is thoroughly misguided with respect to this particular Bill. It is a regressive piece of legislation and it is a tremendous step backward. This piece of legislation comes as no surprise, though. After all, it is the Conservative way of doing things. As far as the Conservative Party is concerned, what is good for General Motors is good for the country. Conservative Members have blind faith in the private sector. With this particular piece of legislation, they have blind faith that foreign investment will enter Canada and provide much needed jobs. After years of slowly and methodically gaining control over our economy, the Tories are prepared to sell our country to foreign interests.
With respect to this particular piece of legislation, the evidence will suggest that 90 per cent of foreign takeovers will go ahead without review. Why is there a need for Bill C-15? The Tories argue that this legislation will lure foreign investment and will create jobs. Yet they have no concrete evidence that that in fact will be the case. I will try to indicate why I believe the opposite may be true.
The Conservative Party also argues that FIRA was a barrier to foreign investment. The facts simply do not bear that out. FIRA was not a barrier to foreign investment. As we are all aware, since its inception in 1974 there were in excess of 6,000 applications. Of those 6,000 applications, 92.2 per cent were approved. In 1977 and again in 1982, certain amendments were made to the Act to streamline the review procedures. Since 1982, 97 per cent of the applications were approved. The Government says that FIRA was a barrier to foreign investment but the facts simply do not bear that out.
FIRA was good legislation. It was not perfect legislation but it was good legislation. That legislation provided that foreign investment was welcome in this country but it had to be of significant benefit to Canada. We in the Liberal Party recognize the benefits of foreign investment. There is good foreign investment and there is bad foreign investment. The Foreign Investment Review Act said to the world that Canada is open for business and wants foreign investment, but we want investment that will be of benefit to Canadians. If it is not of benefit

Investment Canada Act
to Canadians, then we are really not interested. Why, pray tell, would we want foreign investment that would not be beneficial to Canadians from coast to coast?
In my respectful submission, there are even limits to good foreign investment. For example, study after study has shown that foreign-controlled companies do less research and development than domestic companies. Studies also show that most foreign-controlled companies in Canada purchase most of their parts and components from other countries.
FIRA was set up as a review mechanism to ensure that Canada would not suffer as a result of foreign investment. We said that we wanted foreign investment but we insisted that there had to be significant benefit from it. As well, we wanted foreign investment on our terms. What is important is the fact that FIRA gave this country the opportunity to have a very strong negotiating tool with foreign companies which wished to enter the country to do business. We were able to say to these companies that if they wanted to come to Canada to do business, they would have to do it on our terms. They would have to create jobs in the country and would have to do other things that would be of benefit to our economy.
Legislation like FIRA is not unique to Canada. As Hon. Members are aware, there is similar legislation in the U.S., Australia and Japan. These places have extensive controls. For example, in the United States there are very strict controls over whole sectors of the U.S. economy and specifically in the shipping, broadcasting, air transportation and defence components of the economy.
FIRA had the effect it was intended to have. With respect to the recession years, foreign investment increased annually from 1974 onward. Between 1964 and 1973, foreign investment in this country averaged $690 million a year. Since 1974, foreign investment has averaged $1.4 billion each year. In the past four years the average has been $2 billion per year. In 1983 the capital inflow into Canada was $2.8 billion.
What will Investment Canada do? The Government argues that it will create jobs. However, there is no guarantee of more jobs. There is the distinct possibility that foreign companies may enter this country, purchase competitor companies and then close those companies down in order to secure the Canadian market. Is this the result the Government wants? It is inevitable and one must be cautious.
As a result of this new legislation, we will slowly lose control of our economy. There will be a tremendous loss of jobs. As I have already indicated, FIRA was good legislation. It allowed us to gain control over our economy. In every major sector of the economy there was a reduction in the amount of foreign ownership. One need only consult the figures for foreign control of Canadian industry from 1971 to 1981. Mining went from 62 per cent foreign control to 30 per cent. Oil and gas went from 90 per cent foreign control to 49 per cent. Primary metal manufacturing went from 41 per cent foreign control to 13 per cent.
I understand, Mr. Speaker, that my time has expired. I simply wish to say in closing that we in the Liberal Party will fight this legislation every step of the way. In our view it is bad legislation. I would encourage Hon. Members opposite to take a good hard look at the possible serious and detrimental ramifications of Bill C-15.

They are prepared to sell us out faster than the rate of 92 per cent or 97 per cent of the applications. I am concerned that the Conservative Government, in its haste to acquiesce to the United States, is literally going to sell out Canada's opportunities.
We have stated the sins of foreign investment and the failure to establish Canadian control of our economy, as well as what happened during the Liberal regime-the loss of research and development in Canada. That will be accelerated. There is no doubt about it. There will be loss of jobs because of American parent companies shutting down Canadian branch plants. Once they have bought them out, they will simply eliminate competition to their domestic industries in the world

January 24, 1985
Investment Canada Act
market, even in the Canadian market. The purchase of parts and components will further drain money out of this country as well as the purchase of services from the United States, whether engineering, architectural, financial or accounting services, at inflated rates. That will continue to drain more and more money out of Canada.
Again, there is the question of dividends. If we allow foreign investment in, that investment, instead of coming to Canadians to reinvest in Canada, will certainly be sent back to the United States, which will represent substantial job losses for Canadians. We will be effectively following the pattern of the Liberals of destroying the attempt of Canadians to compete in export markets around the world. In fact, this Bill should certainly be hoisted for six months, if not withdrawn.
I see the time now, Mr. Speaker, and I wonder if I might call it one o'clock?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I do not want to disappoint the Hon. Member but I do not think he will call it one o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, I am not, as Hon. Members will know, a frequent speaker in the House, because I often think we can be more effective through our work in parliamentary committees, in caucus, and by travelling across the country to meet Canadians and listen to their major concerns.
My reasons for taking part in the debate today, however- and I will be brief, because our allotted time is very limited, only ten minutes to explain to Canadians what is happening. In other words, at this point we have had eight hours of debate on the main motion and we are now limited to ten minutes. Speed is therefore of the essence.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make several comments. First of all, I would like to talk about Canadian pride and what it means. Second, I would like to respond, without animosity, to my hon. colleague and friend from Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly), who should, I think, read up on the history of Canada and the history of the Liberal Party. Third, I would like to explain how I see this Bill and the dangers I feel it contains.
I have no doubts as to the competence of the Minister sponsoring this legislation. In fact, I know him very well since he was a Member of the Standing Committee on External Affairs which I had the privilege of chairing for a number of years and of which I was a member for nearly twenty years.
The present Minister took an active part in the business of the House and that of the task force on Canada's relations with Latin America, chaired by my colleague from Labelle, Mr. Dupras, who is no longer a Member of the House, not because the voters decided it that way, but of his own volition.
I think it is basically a matter of pride. What does it mean to be Canadian? To be Canadian is not to be anti-American. To be Canadian is not to be anti-British. To be Canadian is not to be anti-French. I put it this way because these are concerns that are close to most Canadians. Our neighbours to the South, the Americans, are our friends, I say it and I say it again, but we do not have to be American! The countries by which this country was founded, France and England . . . England gave us its system of government, and I am very happy with it and 1 will always be ready to defend it because I think it is one of the best political systems in the world. I say it, and I am not afraid to say it, and I am not saying it in English, I am saying it in French, because I believe in the British system. So being proCanadian does not mean being anti-British or anti-French, as I said before. It means that every day, we want to help make our institutions truly Canadian.
You were not here, Mr. Speaker, and very few Members will remember the stormy debates we had, I think it will be twenty years ago next month, about the flag you see on your right. With respect, I may say that the word "right" is very appropriate in your case. The flag was to make us a little more Canadian. There were the traditionalists, and there were those who wanted to develop this idea of Canadianism for the benefit of the young people sitting in front of you, Mr. Speaker, and make Canada a place where our foreign friends, and they are our friends, will not take control of what is ours or undermine our pride in developing the economy of our country as we see fit.
My hon. colleague and friend from Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) put the blame on the Liberals, but he had his facts wrong.
The Liberals don't claim to be the best in the world. There probably are people in Canada who could do better, but they have yet to prove it. As for my friends in the New Democratic Party, they will never get the chance. What he did say however, and he said it very well .. . Actually, I know the Hon. Member from our frequent travels together. I am not so sure he said it in a spirit of friendship, but I do not think he has that much of a grudge against this great political Party that has presided over the destiny of our country and made it the world power it is today, but that is exactly what it means to be a Liberal.
I should perhaps lecture him on what it means to be a Liberal. I see the Hon. Minister of State for Youth (Mrs. Champagne) smile pleasantly. She seems to agree. What does it mean to be a Liberal? I am going to hazard an opinion, Mr. Speaker, and say that it is a matter of balance. In this Bill, a Minister is saying: "Come to Canada, do what you want, and try to create jobs." We do not believe that this Bill will create jobs any more than it will promote research and development in Canada. We have to be very cautious in choosing between a door which is completely open and a door which our friends from the New Democratic Party would like to be completely
January 24, 1985

closed. They refuse everything. They are suspicious of our neighbours to the South, our American friends. For many of them, and I respect them a lot because I have admittedly much in common with their Party, anything American is necessarily bad. I do not share this view. My Party, which has done a lot to make Canada what it is today, does not share this view, nor does it agree with many members of this Government who believe, something which I simply cannot understand, that they just have to say: "Come to Canada, FIRA is no more."
I believe that the mistake of the Liberals was perhaps not to explain well enough to foreign investors, including the Americans who seem to be the ones this Government wants to attract to Canada, what were the true intentions of the review agency we called FIRA. We should have told them that we would behave exactly as they did, our purpose being similar to theirs. As a matter of fact they protect themselves thanks to a very powerful Senate and a very powerful Congress which look carefully at every economic sector in the country for any thing that might harm their businesses. How can these people deny a country as proud as Canada, a country as faithful to its friends, whether it be on military, social or economic matters, as Canada has been to the United States, how can they refuse us what their Congress gives them so easily because of their incredibly powerful lobbies in every industry, including wood and steel?
Mr. Speaker, I am afraid of what will happen to our young people in whom we want to instil a sense of patriotism of which Mr. Reagan spoke so eloquently. I know Mr. Reagan. He came to this Parliament. I saw him. I do not know him well, but I have met him. I have a lot of respect for him because he was able to do something when he was re-elected. He was able to instil a sense of patriotism in his people. Is there anything wrong Mr. Speaker, with making our young people feel proud to be Canadians and with explaining what is in the best interests of Canada? I have two minutes left, Mr. Speaker.
