Mr. Speaker, for several months I have been inundated with letters and phone calls about provisions in the Income Tax Act relating to workmen's compensation and the Guaranteed Income Supplement. I have introduced a notice of motion advising the House to amend the Income Tax Act in order to eliminate the hardships brought about by previous amendments which now make workmen's compensation reportable as income for income tax purposes and GIS purposes.
As many of the Members present are aware, I have been fighting for this change to a law which has greatly affected the already meagre incomes of many of my constituents, particularly senior citizens. It is having far-reaching consequences for many Canadians suffering from economic adversity. Previously this was a special tax break given to our senior citizens. I would urge all Members of this House on all sides, in all political Parties, to consider repealing these provisions of the Act so that it can revert back to the way it was previously.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to bring to your attention and that of this House a change in attitude which I have seen developing in the short time the Progressive Conservatives have formed the Government.
I have in my hand a copy of a letter sent to me by one of my constituents, a Mr. Mike Mallory, concerning a situation which arose in the course of his business. Mr. Mallory originally approached me last fall, concerned about an impending meeting with Canada Customs officials. I assured him that the meeting would be conducted in a most positive, business-like fashion, and I was hopeful his problems could be resolved. I am sure you will be as delighted as I am, Mr. Speaker, to learn that I have recently received a letter from my constituent praising the high level of professionalism and co-operation which he found. This occurred not only in dealing with people from Revenue Canada in the Customs and Excise Branch, but with all members of the Civil Service with whom he came in contact.
I think that all Canadians can be proud of and applaud the situation which has evolved a new spirit of co-operation between Government, the Civil Service, and private industry, one that will surely bode well for all Canadians in years to come.

Hear, hear!

January 24, 1985

Mr. Speaker, I wish to call to the attention of the country the completely irrational plan of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Coates) to buy new uniforms for the Armed Forces at a cost of $36 million. The Minister knows that the majority of people in the Armed Forces have never worn a uniform other than the one they have. He should know that members of all ranks are now criticizing this irrational plan to spend 36 million hard-to-find defence dollars on new and unnecessary uniforms.
I would point out to the Minister that one of the most pressing needs of Canadians from the Department of National Defence is not new coats of many colours, or new, high-tech star wars machines. What we need is more search and rescue helicopters on the West Coast, and the proper deployment of the five existing helicopters at Comox. The Minister knows that the cost of doing that would be only $10 million. Why is the Minister spending $36 million on new suits when $10 million would save lives?

Mr. Speaker, remember November 12, 1981? That was the day the Hon. Allan MacEachen promised equity in the tax system. The legacy of his disastrous Budget will haunt ordinary working Canadians forever. The unfair taxation of travel privileges of Canadian airline employees is just one example. Lost among regressive proposals like the revocation of tax deductions for Canadian pensioners and the attempt to tax Canadian workers on health plan contributions, the taxation of airline passes survives the massive public criticism which swamped the MacEachen Budget.
Here is how the tax measure was implemented. Any employee of a Canadian airline who receives a confirmed seat on a flight and who pays less than half of the regular economy fare would be taxed on the difference between the amount paid and 50 per cent of this fare.
This week Air Canada announced its new Red Tag fares. To travel from Toronto to Vancouver the new fare is $299 compared to the regular economy fare of $810, a reduction of more than 60 per cent. In the result, an ordinary Canadian travels for less than 40 per cent of the regular economy fare and pays no extra tax. An Air Canada employee paying the same fare is taxed on an alleged benefit of $106.
The former Liberal Minister of Finance has gone to his political reward, but airline employees will pay for his mistakes.

The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) has placed great importance on Canada remaining silent, which can only be interpreted as support for star wars research and the escalating that will flow from it. The Minister believes in the theology that, once negotiations start, Canadian anxiety over star wars research should not be expressed for fear that our views would disrupt negotiations. He also believes that it is virtuous to resist pressures from home and refrain at any cost from conveying to the United States Government Canadian concerns on this very important issue.
This argument is spurious but, be that as it may, the Minister owes an explanation to this House and the country as to why, on the one hand, he is supportive of research programs in outer space which may one day destroy all of us, but fails to increase Canada's contribution to the United Nations environment program whose role is to find ways and means of protecting the environment on this planet and ultimately the protection of all of humanity.
If outer space research is to go on for the sake of negotiations, why does the Minister not at least ensure that environmental research at home and abroad, and through the UN environment program, is awarded the same support by the Government as it is now giving the star wars program?

subtopic: CANADIAN FORCES BASE CHATHAM-PROTECTION OF JOBS
CANADIAN FORCES BASE CHATHAM-PROTECTION OF JOBS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, concerning the Department of National Defence let me say that with this Government a commitment made is a commitment kept. Some three years ago the Minister of National Defence of the day announced the stand-down of the operational squadron at Canadian Forces Base Chatham. That came like a bombshell because there was no other commitment, statement, or solution to the plight of hundreds of public servants who stood to lose their jobs. I believe the Minister's statement at the time was something to the effect that it was a wonderful opportunity for them to use their initiative. Well, they did, Mr. Speaker. For the first time in 42 years they turned out in record numbers to vote, and vote Conservative.
Just before Christmas our Minister of National Defence (Mr. Coates) kept faith with the people of New Brunswick, kept faith with the people of Miramichi, by announcing a military package that will ensure the jobs, livelihood, and future of these loyal public servants well into the next century. On their behalf I thank the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of National Defence for keeping the faith and for keeping a promise.
January 24, 1985
Mr. Speaker, the antiwest bias continues under Conservatives.
Oh, oh!

In spite of loud proclamations from the Conservative Party and its Leader before the election, and more since forming the Government, about a better deal for western Canada, this Government continues the ways of the old Liberal regime by allowing the removal of services from western cities, and by continuing the discriminatory actions of the previous Government.
The three latest slaps to western Canada are the removal of 43 Air Canada reservations employees from Regina and Saskatoon, some to Winnipeg and some to the unemployment line, and Air Canada's refusal to allow low-price seat sales in these same two cities. In addition, the Ministry of Transport intends to remove the RCMP security officers from Regina airport.
The Liberals denuded Regina of weather forecasters, air traffic controllers, customs and excise personnel, our income tax files, and now the Conservatives are continuing this discriminatory treatment. We call on the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) to do his duty to his native west and use his powers to require Air Canada to retain its reservations offices in Regina and Saskatoon, offer seat sales in Saskatchewan, and maintain the RCMP officers on security duty at Regina airport, the city which is their home and the home of the RCMP.
The Tories promised us jobs. When are they going to deliver them, instead of getting rid of them?

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to express my views on the new nuclear defence system proposed by President Regan.
The Star Wars project of the American President, which has the support of the Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark), is a revolutionary concept in defensive weaponry whose purpose in the long run is to make it possible to eradicate all nuclear missiles from the surface of the earth or at least to prevent their constant proliferation which has been worrying us for several years.
I am surprised that the Opposition should be so bitterly critical of a project which would allow us to reduce substantially the likelihood of a holocaust. This weapon system is much more moral than any other because its aim is to destroy enemy weapons and not people. Confrontation with our
American neighbours has been the attitude of the opposition for many years. This program has unleashed many passions. Certain experts question the fact that the Americans and their allies will ever be able to develop this new technology. They say that the basic principle, which is to install in space a 100-meter mirror 36,000 kilometers from earth, is unworkable. Of course, the risks are great and often impossible to evaluate, but it is important to believe in our potential. We have to support a partner which is spending enormous amounts of money for our security.
Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that the Canadian people will understand and support our position, which is realistic and basically humane, because where weapons are concerned morality is not to allow one's destruction by claiming one is a pacifist, but rather by choosing the lesser of two evils.
I am sorry to interrupt the Hon. Member, but his time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government plans to create a super information agency in an effort tantamount to creating a Pravda Canada.
The year 1984 may be over, but the spirit of George Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four is alive, well, and living within the Conservative Government. The Tory Big Brother, the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen), has imposed his authoritarian presence in all Government Departments. Typically, he has done it in the same covert manner which marked previous Tory communications schemes, such as the Public Service gag order imposed last September.
The Conservative Government is also continuing its arrogant and cynical disregard for promises and commitments made to Canadians prior to the election. The Conservatives in opposition were vocally opposed to Information Canada a decade ago, and opposed to the Canadian Unity Information Office. In Government, they are creating a giant system which dwarfs the Canadian Unity Information Office. Instead of open government, the Conservatives are providing closed government, in which all information is to be carefully manipulated by central government, real Big Brother government.
The centralized information agency will also further the politicization of the Public Service by putting major government information programs in the hands of the private sector. A fitting name for the super agency would indeed be Pravda Canada.

January 24, 1985

maintopic: CALL FOR INSTALLATION OF RADAR AT VICTORIA INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT
CALL FOR INSTALLATION OF RADAR AT VICTORIA INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week the Ministry of Transport issued a press release describing the impending improvements to double the passenger handling facilities over the next 18 months at Victoria International Airport. The announcement indicated that possibly radar would be installed as early as 1987 or 1988.
Victoria Airport serves the provincial capital. Greater Victoria is a tourist mecca. Victoria International Airport is as described, an international airport, and is an emergency or diversion airport for Vancouver. Victoria is one of the ten busiest airports in Canada.
Radar, an essential safety device, is long overdue and long promised. I urge most strenuously that the Government reconsider its timetable and install this most necessary equipment as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, one can only approve of recent announcements by the Minister of Transport pertaining to the reinstatement of passenger rail services that were cancelled by the Liberals, and one can only hope that the announced intention to upgrade, modernize, and expand passenger rail service will be followed up with real money and concrete action.
However, if such modernization and upgrading do take place, then sooner or later VIA must have a new repair facility in the West, and in Winnipeg in particular, if logic and common sense are to be heeded. I therefore regret that the VIA repair shop scheduled to be built in Winnipeg appears to be on indefinite hold, or even cancelled.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) ought not to make the same mistake made by the former Minister of Transport, the Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), and be tempted to allocate such facilities on a political basis. It was the selection of the Fort Rouge site in Winnipeg, which just happened to be in the riding of the Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry, over other potential sites, without consulting the city or the railways, that endangered the project in the first place. The City of Winnipeg then compounded the problem with delay, thereby giving the new Conservative Government the opportunity to play its own brand of politics with the project.
I call on the present Minister of Transport to rise above the politics of the issue, show the foresight that I know he is capable of, and ensure that Winnipeg is indeed the place for new VIA facilities in the West.

subtopic: TENDERING PROCESS FOR EXPO PAVILION CONTRACT
TENDERING PROCESS FOR EXPO PAVILION CONTRACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to bring to the attention of the House a matter concerning Air Canada. This was brought to my attention by a segment of the construction industry. Air Canada has used a method of select tendering for its Expo pavilion, which is perfectly legal and which it is free to do.
However, as a result of its selection process there has been the elimination of 10 to 12 companies that were interested in submitting a tender for the pavilion. The non union firms, of which there were two, were also not invited to submit a tender. I am suspicious of why the non union firms were excluded. Perhaps Air Canada feels that non union firms are incapable of building pavilions at Expo, even though a number of pavilions have already been awarded to non union firms. I fail to see how Air Canada's tender selection process can be the most cost effective if competition among firms is minimized.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last December the Right Hon. Prime Minister of Canada made it clear that constitutional talks with Quebec were not a high priority for his Government.
This morning, the newspaper Le Devoir reported that apparently the Prime Minister was now prepared to start constitutional talks with Quebec and to accelerate the process.
My question to the Prime Minister is as follows: Since at its convention last weekend, the Parti Quebecois decided that the issue of sovereignty or independence would not be part of its election program in the next provincial election, and since, according to Premier Levesque, an election would be held in a matter of months, is it true that the Prime Minister of Canada is prepared to resume constitutional talks with Quebec with a view to reaching an agreement with the Quebec Government before the next election?

Mr. Speaker, I do not think I said anything about encouraging the kind of proposals reported in Le Devoir or elsewhere.
I was asked yesterday whether I thought Mr. Levesque had a mandate to negotiate. I said: Of course. He is the duly elected Premier of Quebec and he has a mandate to negotiate in constitutional as well as economic matters. The fact that he
January 24, 1985

is nearing the end of his term does not in any way restrict, I would think, the scope of his mandate.
That being said, we have always stated that our concern was basically economic, but we certainly would not prevent the premier of a province from submitting proposals in another area.
This was in connection with a meeting we had with Mr. Levesque, at which he indicated his priorities and said he might be submitting some constitutional proposals after Easter. I said at the time that I would be delighted, as the Prime Minister of Canada, to consider objectively such proposals.
I still believe that Quebec's concerns are basically economic, but I am nevertheless willing to meet with the Premier of Quebec at any time with a view to seeking a formula for bringing Quebec within a Canadian constitutional agreement.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister referred to Mr. Levesque's mandate. He must be aware that in a motion passed by the National Assembly of Quebec on November 24, 1981, the Government of Quebec laid down its conditions for resumption of constitutional talks. Could the Prime Minister of Canada inform the House what his Government intends to put on the table to show its good faith, after the gesture made by the Parti Quebecois, the Quebec Government, last weekend, in order to achieve a speedy integration of Quebec within the new constitutional framework created following patriation of the Canadian Constitution?

Mr. Speaker, I think it may be somewhat premature and even undiplomatic on my part to submit any proposals when it is understood, as Mr. Levesque said himself in Quebec City, that the ball is in his court. And he was right. It is true that a number of proposals were adopted by the National Assembly in the fall of 1981, which probably will be part of a constitutional discussion. I am aware of that, and after Easter I will be ready to consider the situation outlined by Mr. Levesque, and see if the proposals are still the same, whether any minor or major changes have been made.

Press reports this week have suggested that the Government may be considering unilateral action on the matter of compensation to the Japanese-Canadian community for the injustice that community suffered during the Second World War. subsubtopic: INTERNMENT OF JAPANESE CANADIANS DURING WORLD WAR II-COMPENSATION INQUIRY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in reply to the Hon. Member, the Government is attempting to pursue what we consider and what we hope is a just and honourable course. I hope that the Hon. Member and his Party, and members of the Liberal Party, join us in what I believe is a very worth-while task and objective.

What I indicated to the press this morning is that the Government House Leader is in the process of having discussions with the opposition House Leaders. Until those
discussions are completed, I am not in a position and I will not comment publicly on what may or may not transpire.

Mr. Speaker, given the complexity of the issues involved in this matter of appropriate redress to the Japanese-Canadian community, will the Minister assure the House that the Government will not take any action before it has arrived at an agreement with the National Association of Japanese Canadians?

Mr. Speaker, we have attempted to have as broad-ranging a discussion on this very important matter as is possible. As I indicated to the Hon. Member, certainly later today, and if not today, tomorrow, hopefully, the discussions can be concluded so that this House of Commons may proceed in some form at least to acknowledge what I think we all would agree has been something long overdue in this country.
Forty-three years.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Minister of State for Multiculturalism. Given the statement from his own Ministry in December that a process of negotiation had begun, and given that there have been only a couple of meetings since then which served to explore the parameters of various questions and came nowhere near to an agreement, will the Minister assure this House and the National Association of Japanese Canadians that he will not impose early deadlines as a way of forcing an agreement on something that is so important to national honour?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member knows, I believe, and so does the National Association of Japanese-Canadians, as do the Japanese-Canadians themselves, that what we entered into in December was a discussion with them, not a negotiation of any sort. They know that. The Hon. Member knows that. In my opinion we have had fruitful discussions. We have been able to set down both sides of the issues. As I said to the Hon. Member in my two previous answers, we hope that this matter will be dealt with in the House of Commons by all Members in a very appropriate and honourable way in the near future.
January 24, 1985
, main CONDITION FOR QUEBEC ACCEPTANCE OF CONSTITUTIONAL AGREEMENT

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Right Hon. Prime Minister and stems from an article published this morning in the Montreal daily Le Devoir. Could the Prime Minister indicate to the House whether he finds acceptable the first condition set by Quebec's Assemblee nationale as a prerequisite to signing the Constitutional agreement and which reads as follows: "It should be recognized that the two founding nations of Canada are basically equal and that Quebec forms within the Canadian federation a distinct society which has its own language, culture, and institutions, and which possesses all the attributes of a distinct national entity"? If he does not find it acceptable, what changes does he think should be made, so that Quebec might sign the Constitutional agreement as soon as possible?

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member knows full well that I cannot answer such a hypothetical question. I think that on such a vital issue as the Constitutional dialogue, we should avoid ambiguity at all costs. Elementary caution demands that I await, as agreed with Mr. Levesque, the specific written proposals which Quebec is to submit after Easter. Once we have had the opportunity to study and analyse them thoughtfully, I shall tell my counterpart what I think of these proposals as a whole and not only on some isolated parameter.

I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. The question which I have just directed to the Prime Minister is in no way a hypothetical question. It has to do with a specific motion that has been passed unanimously by the Assemblee nationale. I should like to ask the Prime Minister under what terms ... I suggest that it is a thoroughly valid condition which could serve as an interesting basis for discussion. It seems to me that if the Prime Minister would indicate to the House and to the Canadian people under what terms his government is planning to negotiate-because for negotiations to happen both sides have to forward proposals-if he could give us some indication on such a simple matter, that could facilitate the forthcoming debate.

What we are trying to do, Mr. Speaker, is to restore a climate of confidence between the Federal government and the Quebec government, between all Quebecers and all other Canadians, and I suggest things are developing rather nicely. We are building bridges of trust and trying to bury the Liberal tradition of systematic mistrust which has existed far too long in Canada. That is what we are trying to do.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
speechtext:
The Temporary Assignment Program was established in 1974. The intention was to create a centrally managed pool of executives and other senior officers of demonstrated high levels of performance who could be loaned to departments on request, individually or in teams, for specific periods of time, to carry out policy reviews and similar activities without the need for, delay in, or cost associated with establishing continuing positions in those departments.
In the 10 years since its inception, participants in the program, which is managed on a cost recovery basis by Treasury Board Secretariat, have completed a total of 377 assignments in 54 departments.
(a)	During the period from April 1, 1983 through November 30, 1983, the number of persons employed in the Temporary Assignment Program ranged from 37 to 41.
(b)	From December 2, 1983 to November 30, 1984, there were from 33 to 40 persons employed in the Temporary Assignment Program.
Effective November 30, 1984, (i) the salary level and (ii) duties of TAP's participants were as follows:
(i) Three officials with salaries ranging from $68,870 to $80,970 (EX 4 level), thirteen officials with salaries ranging from $63,000 to 74,050 (EX 3 level), seven officials with salaries ranging from $58,050 to $68,500 (EX 2 level), five officials with salaries ranging from $53,210 to $62,530 (EX 1 level), seven officials with salaries ranging from $50,350 to $59,220 (SM level).

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Stevens that Bill C-15, an Act respecting investment in Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Regional Development; and on the amendment of Mr. Gray (Windsor West) (p. 1302).

Mr. Speaker, I welcome very much this opportunity to make a few comments with respect to Bill C-15. I am pleased to see my friend, the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens), the Hon. Member for York-Peel, in the House today.
This change of name from FIRA, Foreign Investment Review Agency, to Investment Canada, Mr. Speaker, is very much in keeping with the kind of approach which this Government has taken to date with respect to matters of government. Rhetoric, name changes, cosmetics rather than substance, seem really to be the order of the day when it comes to the policies or, I should say, lack thereof of the Tory Government since it assumed office on September 4. As Shakespeare said, a rose by any other name would smell as sweet, and I suggest that that is the underlying theme of what the Minister is trying to accomplish.
We were already told by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney), during the election campaign when he was Leader of the Opposition, that as soon as Knowlton Nash on television tells us the Tories have formed a majority Government, investment is going to flow into this country. I think in fact he actually believed that. However, Mr. Speaker, as you know from your experience in public life and as a Member of this House for some years, history has shown us how nervous capital can be. You can scare capital through rhetoric of the kind we heard from the Parti Quebecois. It is very easy to destroy confidence through rhetoric coming from responsible people in public life. It is much more difficult, however, Mr. Speaker, to instil confidence, to create an investment climate,
simply through changing names and advancing rhetoric for consumption by Canadians and foreigners. We know that the warm Tory overtures to members of the business and investment communities have in fact produced nothing except warm expressions of appreciation.
I believe the Tories by this time should recognize that it requires more than name changes, rhetoric and dealing with Investment Canada; it involves dealing with a whole set of policies, none of which we have seen as yet. In fact, it is shameful when one considers that this Government assumed power in Canada on September 4 and we have to wait seven to eight months for a budget. We must wait that long for a budget from a Government which said: "When we arrive there, boy, are we going to do things". It has 211 elected Members to do those things. The Government was given a mandate by the Canadian people and it has refused to accept it.
As we in this House know, Mr. Speaker, and as Canadians soon will begin to recognize, I know this gang is not ready to govern Canada, but it is ready to offer us rhetoric, some tinkering around the edges, modifications and so on.
With respect to this particular Bill, Mr. Speaker, I attempted to actually read it in order to determine whether it really does what the accompanying literature says it does. I have come to the conclusion that perhaps it does but I cannot tell because it is so badly drafted. This document would give the Income Tax Act a run for its money, yet this is a document, Mr. Speaker, which is intended to simplify and streamline procedures and, we are told, to facilitate investment and create confidence.
I wanted to find out what the reviewable transactions really were so I turned to Clause 14, which provides:
(1) The following investments by non-Canadians are reviewable under this Part:
(a)	an investment to acquire control of a Canadian business in any manner described in paragraph 28(l)(a), (*) or (c), where the limits set out in subsection (3) apply;
(b)	an investment to acquire control of a Canadian business in the manner described in subparagraph 28( 1 )(</)('), where the limits set out in subsection (3) apply;
(c)	an investment to acquire control of a Canadian business in the manner described in subparagraph 28(l)(d)(ii), where the circumstances described in subsection (2) and the limits set out in subsection (3) apply; and
Finally we go on to another section where the limits set out as Subclause (4) apply, and the clause continues. My point is, Mr. Speaker, that this is a convoluted, complicated piece of legislation which in effect does nothing to simplify procedures.
I had an interesting conversation yesterday with a former colleague at the bar, who said his colleagues had been struggling to interpret sections of this new, simplified, streamlined Act which has been produced by the Conservative Government. We are told these initiatives are going to create jobs, and I can say to you, Mr. Speaker, that they are going to create a lot of jobs for the lawyers of this country who must once more educate themselves in the interpretation of this statute to determine whether or not it applies to the circumstances of their clients. This Government has indeed created

Members across the House and on either side know, that the reason those jobs are being created is because of the economic legacy left by the previous Government. More specifically, jobs are being created because of the rate of inflation which is driving down interest rates and encouraging investments. It has nothing whatsoever to do with anything this Government has done because in effect this Government has done nothing to date. However, this document will add thousands of man-hours of non-productive professional work simply to determine whether a particular investment is reviewable or not.
The Government would have us believe the whole operation is simpler. That is the rhetoric we hear. So far Canadians have given the Tories the benefit of the doubt. They have, if you like, been seeing things but not observing. They have been hearing things but they really have not been listening. They have not attempted to measure the performance of this Government against the rhetoric. If I were to characterize the attitude of the Canadian public today, they see but they do not listen. How else can we explain the widening gulf between the declarations of Government spokesmen on this Bill with what it in substance actually is? This has been happening since the Tories assumed power. It is nothing new.
Let me offer a few examples, if I may, just to underscore the point. The Tories heaped blame and ridicule on the previous Liberal Government because of what they called corporate bail-outs. Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to participate once more in this important debate. I think we have reached the stage where it is interesting to reflect on what has been taking place during this debate.
I think at first there was a sense on the part of the Government that it would be able to whip this Bill very quickly through the House, get it into committee and passed. In fact, the Minister was even courageous enough at one point to say that he expected everything to be passed by the middle of March. I think, Mr. Speaker, that things are taking place in the country which make that prospect less and less likely.
As this debate has unfolded, Mr. Speaker, we have seen the Government first try to get across a very simple, indeed simplistic, message-that this Bill, simply through its introduction and the changes it makes, will give us an extra $1 billion in new investment in Canada. The Government has tried to tell us there would be many new jobs created and that those of us oppose the Bill are somehow out of step, old-fashioned nationalists who are leading with our hearts instead of our heads.
Our response has been, in a sense, equally simple. The response has been to say that foreign investment is not part of the solution to our economic problems, that indeed controlling foreign investment is part of the problem. Unrestricted foreign investment is part of the problem because of the way foreign-controlled firms import from the parent company instead of buying in Canada. It is part of the problem because of high capital outflows that foreign investment creates. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly), indicated this morning that over $2 million leaves this country each and every hour of each and every day as a result of foreign investment. So we have stated our simple sloganistic response to the Government's slogan of Investment Canada, that Bill C-15 is about Warehouse Canada. It is about establishing a branch plant economy even more than in the past and that will badly damage the jobs we so desperately need.
As I reflect on this debate, Mr. Speaker, I have a sense that we are moving into a new phase in which the public are now starting to recognize what has been happening with this Bill. I have just come back from three days of listening to groups, individuals and communities throughout Atlantic Canada. I can tell this House that there is a concern, a sense of unease, in provinces like Newfoundland and places like Cape Breton which have experienced what unrestricted foreign private investment can do to a community. They have experienced the shutdown of mines and mills and they are concerned that this Government is once more taking the country in that direction.
One sign of that concern is that on February 9, just a few weeks away, a group of people who want to give new momentum to the old Canadians For An Independent Canada are once more meeting. They are going to re-establish that organization and use it in what will become an increasing public fight against this effort to take away our first line of defence against foreign control and the problems it can bring to our economy. The letters come in every day from the people I talk to in my constituency and others. They come in from Ontario,

Investment Canada Act
from Atlantic Canada, and express their concern and unease. I think we will see as this debate continues that more and more Canadians recognize that what this Government is trying to do with this Bill is not to give us more jobs. It is trying to give more favours to the foreign investors who have always supported it in the past to whom it feels it owes favours in return after its election victory.
As our New Democratic Party action group on jobs moves throughout the country, another impression that I have is that the pot of gold approach to economic planning for our country, as referred to by Richard Cashin of the Fishermen's Union in Newfoundland, no longer makes sense. The idea of opening ourselves up and giving the invitation to come in and use our resources and build on Canadian benefits as the answer to our problems is one that I do not believe Canadians are interested in. I do not believe that people are interested in that kind of imported solution to the problems we face.
Instead, what I see and hear as an increasing theme throughout the country is a desire for self-reliance. It is a desire for community based and directed efforts to build our economy.
In Newfoundland it takes the form of new co-ops that are building jobs and playing the role that private foreign investment has never historically been able to play in much of our country and will not be able to play. In Glace Bay it takes the form of an attempt to set up what they call incubator malls, which are small scale malls that give small businesses a chance to serve community and Canadian needs and provide Canadian solutions.
We have seen a rather different direction in which this country wants to move. It is a direction which is totally undermined by Bill C-15, and we will continue to fight to make sure that Bill C-15 is abandoned and that a new approach of self-reliance and community direction is increasingly adopted.

The Government says that it is trying to promote jobs. The Government is welcoming capital into Canada to buy industries. I have nothing against foreign capital coming into Canada. But I do not want to see foreign companies control many of our Canadian industries. They must remain under Canadian control. I know there are clauses in the Bill dealing with this, but it is a much looser situation that even existed with F1RA.
This Tory Government should look at history and look to the days of the Arrow aircraft and the plant I just mentioned, Haley Industries. It made parts for the Arrow aircraft. What happened? The Tory Government of the day scrapped the whole plan, and even took the moulds out of the foundry at Haley Industries. The moulds were taken out into the back yard and smashed so they would not be used again. That is the kind of progress we see in job-making and future technology from a Conservative Government. If that program had been allowed to go ahead, we would not be bringing foreign capital into Canada in large globs today and we would not be shipping out our cash to buy aircraft. Instead, we would be selling the Arrow aircraft, which was one of the best aircraft built in the world and it would still be modern in terms of any aircraft that exists today. But the last Conservative Government destroyed one of the best domestic industries we had going in this country, and today we are buying an aircraft from the United States at a cost of billions of dollars to the Canadian taxpayer. That is what the Tories call progress. Here we have a Bill before us today ironically a Bill called Investment Canada.
What has happened in the area of wood products, Mr. Speaker? In that great area of Algonquin Park in the upper Ottawa Valley and in areas of northern Ontario, we have had foreign companies come in and be given leases by the provincial Government. One particular company from the United States took up a large section of good woodland in that area that contained some of the best timber. The company was from Missouri. It sat on the timber. Local companies in Canada could not even buy timber and if they did, they not only had to pay the dues which went normally to the Ontario Government but they also had to pay dues to the foreign company in Missouri. That is hardly progress. That can hardly be called Investment Canada. But that was done under a Tory Government in the Province of Ontario. We have so much talk about the fact that we must build up our forests, but this is something that should have been talked about years ago.
We did and you Liberals wouldn't listen.

The management of forests is in the hands of provincial governments. They have been destroying them for years. They have been selling them off for foreign capital. They have not been encouraging local entrepreneurs to get involved in the secondary industrial process in the wood industry in this country.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are giving me a signal. I shall try to accommodate you. If we are going to have a Conserva-
Investment Canada Act
tive Government in this country with 211 Members bringing in a Bill called Investment Canada, then let us have some better examples of progress in developing industry in Canada, developing industry for Canadians by Canadians, and let us see some of those tens of thousands of jobs that we were promised we would get the day after the election. Here we are back again after all the criticism about all the short-term programs and yet we have Canada Works about to be announced, a Liberal program. Mr. Speaker, the Conservatives call this Bill Investment Canada. I call it Betrayal Canada. If ever there was a time to learn from history so as not to be condemned to repeat it, it is in the area of foreign investment in this country.
It is always desirable to have a measure of foreign investment. Canada historically has leaned over backwards to get foreign investment, to the extent that even the Liberals had to quit some of their supine acquiescence to foreign investments, particularly United States investments. We learned some bitter lessons in this country because of the amount of foreign ownership of our economy.
I believe a larger portion of foreign investment should be loan capital and a smaller portion of it should be equity or ownership capital. I give as an example what we did in my Province of Saskatchewan with a publicly owned power corporation. In almost ten years we increased massively our electrical generating capacity. We took electricity to every town and village in the province. We electrified 60,000 farms and borrowed something over $600 million in that time, most of it foreign money, but it was loan capital. The foreign investors who lent money to the Saskatchewan Power Corporation got a good and reasonable return on their investment. Those loans have been paid off and the people of Saskatchewan own their power corporation. Contrast that, Mr. Speaker, with other public-type utilities that are foreign-owned or foreign-con-trolled.
There is a lot of investment capital available here in Canada. I do not blame the U.S. corporations for the way they behave up here. We are to blame. Foreign investors need to know in advance what our ground rules are. We need firm ground rules that they know ahead of time. As long as they can make a reasonable return on their investment, they will live up to those ground rules. Taking the ground rules away just encourages more of what has occurred in the past.
Let me give an example of one of the experiences Canada had in the 1960s regarding foreign investment. Chrysler Corporation of Windsor, Ontario, had an opportunity to sell several hundred trucks to Cuba. The parent company, Chrysler of the United States, was told by the United States Government that it was not to allow its branch plant in Canada to sell trucks to Cuba. It was called Trading with the Enemy Act. There was the United States Government telling a corporation with its head office in the U.S. that Canadian workers and a Canadian plant could not produce and sell

January 24, 1985
Investment Canada Act
trucks to another country. That is a direct intrusion into our sovereignty and our independence. This type of thing has occurred countless times. The more we open up to foreign investment, as the Government proposes to do, the more we will have these occurrences.
There is lots of Canadian capital to be invested in Canada. Why do we not clean up our own house before starting to worry about how much foreign investment is coming in?
You may not be aware, Mr. Speaker, that there are some $35 billion of corporation tax deferrals lying on the books of the Government of Canada which will never be paid. We do not even collect interest on it. If one charged a modest 9 per cent or 10 per cent, the Government could do something more about medicare, hospitalization, housing and a few other things. What has happened with these corporate tax deferrals? Let me give you an illustration, Mr. Speaker.
Canadian capital has been taken out of Canada by the hundreds of millions of dollars for investment in other places. For example, Great Lakes Paper, a subsidiary of Canadian Pacific Limited, has something in the order of $150 million in corporate tax deferrals. It has received federal and provincial grants of $50 million to upgrade its plant production facilities in northwestern Ontario. What did it do? It invested $25 million in the United States to build a pulp and paper plant. Surely that is not good corporate behaviour or good corporate citizenship. Canadian jobs are being exported to the United States. Why? It is because Great Lakes Paper, a subsidiary of Canadian Pacific, wants to take the fullest advantage of our corporate tax laws, to the disadvantage of Canada. At least it should be made to give back the $50 million so that we can let someone else in Canada invest in a pulp and paper production facility here.
Canadian Pacific owes $1.5 billion in deferred corporation taxes. In theory, the corporation takes that money and invests it in fixing up its plant, in new equipment, more production, new technology and Canadian jobs. Well, that company invested it all right. All the years Canadian Pacific obtained corporate tax deferrals it was investing. It bought a pottery plant in Syracuse, New York for $20 million. It has parking lots, shopping centres and condominiums in California. It has mines in Central America and in other parts of the world. It does oil and gas exploration in other parts of the world. That is what it did with its benefits. That is not good corporate citizenship. That capital should have been invested in Canada. Corporations such as Canadian Pacific need to be told that they have to act as good Canadian corporate citizens and invest here where investments are needed.
We rely more than we need on foreign investment because of a system which allows corporations to act in such a manner in this country. International Nickel is another company which owes about $1.5 billion in corporate taxes. It has invested too. Where? It invested in Guatemala, Indonesia and Chile. It took the money and ran with it, money it was supposed to invest in its operations here.
As I said, I do not blame American corporations for acting in that manner. If an American parent company in the United States finds that it has too much production and that it has to shut down plants, it is perfectly natural for it not to shut down plants in its own country. It will shut down branch plants in other countries, namely in Canada. I do not blame those companies for that. Those are the ground rules. Naturally such corporations will take actions in the interests of their own country and their own parent company first, and the host company in which they invest gets second consideration. That has been endemic over the decades of our history. The first ones to get it in the neck are foreign-owned branch plants.
FIRA was weak enough. It was a toothless tiger. It allowed investments which should not have been allowed. It failed to work at getting more Canadian investment. I just sat back quietly while foreign investment came in that we neither wanted nor needed and that could have been filled by Canadian investment. It also cost us in the export of capital from the country by way of dividends and interest. I do not object to investors making a reasonable return on investment, but in many instances they have taken back to their home country three to four times as much as their original investment.
I noticed in an English language newspaper published in Mexico City a report of the experience of Mexico with $1.2 billion of American investment over a period of three years. American investors took $4.5 billion out of Mexico. It is a poor country. Most of its people are poor. That is the benefit it received from foreign investment.
The time is past when we should be laying out ground rules which are reasonable, fair and in the best interests of Canadian sovereignty, independence and jobs. Foreign investors, knowing the ground rules ahead of time, knowing they will receive fair and honest treatment, and knowing that they will be eligible for a reasonable return on investment, will be willing to invest loan capital or equity capital. To throw open the doors so that foreign investors can come and go as they please is surely not in the best interests of Canada's nationhood or of jobs for Canadian people. The instances which we have seen recently with Great Lakes Paper and other examples which could be cited show once again that this blind, irresponsible crawling on hands and knees to got foreign investment at the expense of our sovereignty and independence has to be stopped.
We hope the Government will reconsider this legislation and that it will not only maintain an investment review agency-I do not care what it is called-but will strengthen it and make it more effective than anything we have had before.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in the debate on the Investment Canada Bill. At the outset I want to state that Hon. Members of the Opposition should feel pleased that the Government has at least acknowledged the value of having some form of foreign investment review. Without the evolution of both opposition Parties over the years, there would never have been public awareness of the need for a review of foreign investment in Canada.
January 24, 1985

I should like to refer to some of the background. Until roughly 1952 most of the foreign investment in Canada was in the form of portfolios, bonds and pension fund management. However, beginning in that year and going through a series of both Liberal and Conservative Governments, there was a growing awareness by Canadians of the importance and implications of having significant sectors of our economy dominated by foreign investment. For example, over the years from 1952 to roughly 1971, foreign ownership, largely American ownership, in some key sectors such as energy-not too much in financial institutions-and transportation made succeeding Governments become more aware of some of the bad side effects of foreign investment in our economy.
Some of the rhetoric from the government side would indicate that, since 1971 and because of the fact we began in 1972 with the Foreign Investment Review Agency, in fact there has been a decrease in the amount of foreign investment in Canada. With the exception of 1981, when the National Energy Program played a significant role in the net export of Canadian capital in order to have Canadian ownership of the energy field, foreign investment in Canada has continued to flow in despite the existence of FIRA. After listening to the government side one would think Canada was the only country in the western industrialized world which had at its disposal a tool such as FIRA.
For people who are following the debate, it is interesting to note that there are other countries in the western world which, over the years, have found it necessary to restrict foreign investment in key sectors of their economy for the purpose of protecting the national interests of those countries. In the United States, whole sectors of its economy, such as shipping, broadcasting, air transport and all defence production, are simply off limits to foreign control. Australia has a foreign investment review board which is very similar to FIRA. I need not remind Canadians that the Japanese have extensive controls and foreign investment. These were two examples which I wanted to cite.
Other countries have seen it to be in their best national interest to have some direct government control of the amount of foreign investment entering their borders. I want to point to the United States and get into some greater detail. In the United States, any foreign investment in shipping on the coastal and fresh water systems is strictly prohibited. The shipbuilding industry is barred from government benefits. I could go on and on. Television operators and nuclear power facilities are prohibited from foreign investment.
There are some very good reasons why national governments enact legislation in order to have some form of control over foreign investment within their boundaries. One would like to ask the question about the prospects for future foreign investment in Canada. In a speech which the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made in New York some six weeks ago, he gave the impression that no foreign dollars flowed into Canada during the administration of Prime Minister Trudeau and Prime
Investment Canada Act
Minister Turner and that it is only since the election of the Conservative Government on September 4 that one can expect, because of the new open mat policy of the Conservative Government, that billions of dollars of foreign investment will flow into Canada as a result of the so-called changes in the Foreign Investment Review Agency, replacing it with the Investment Canada Act.
If that is the premise, one should look at what is expected in the United States between 1986 and 1990. If you look at the flow of investment originating in the United States for the past 30 years, you find that beginning in the mid-seventies the United States has changed from a net exporter of capital to a net importer of capital during those years. In fact, the international debt accumulated by the United States during the past few years will fully offset all international assets built up over the last 30 years.
That will change.

The Member say that will change. One can have that optimism, but clearly the Conservative Government has embarked on a direction which it hopes will result in the creation of thousands upon thousands of jobs domestically in Canada as a result of the inflow of capital. From the standpoint of Canadians, I hope the Government's optimism will show in results as well as in rhetoric. If not, I remind Members opposite that there will be several Members on this side of the House who will kindly remind the Government about the promises it made during the last election campaign and the complete faith they have placed in the ability of foreign investment to come through on behalf of Canadian interests.
Some of that faith has been misplaced. I will review for the purposes of Members opposite some of the results of the way in which foreign subsidiaries have operated in Canada. The facts do not justify the faith they have placed in the ability of foreign investment to come through in terms of Canadian interests in this country. Time after time there have been cases in which research and development in the subsidiary has been cut back at the expense of Canadian jobs so that the home company, particularly in the United States, could maintain its research and development with respect to its home borders.
I need not go any further than to suggest the case of the Iron Ore Company of Canada. Decisions made in another country, namely the United States, adversely impacted on its subsidiary operations in Canada. I am not suggesting that the particular case of Iron Ore should be dealt with any differently than in other areas. However, I would suggest that the fact that Canadian-controlled firms have, to a large extent, protected Canadian self-interests in other than research and development and employment opportunities indicates to me that we should not place all our faith in the ability of parent firms lying outside our national borders to look after our best interests.
Lastly, one may wish to investigate some of the proposals which the Conservative Government has in its Investment Canada Bill which are significantly different from the Foreign Investment Review Agency which was created by past Liberal

January 24, 1985
Investment Canada Act
administrations. Evidently it will remove the requirement that we had previously to show significant Canadian content and reason for investing in Canadian firms. In addition to the mandate of the agency for the undertaking of investment performance reviews for foreign-controlled and Canadian firms and of policy development to increase the autonomy of Canadian subsidaries, there are things we proposed in the last election campaign that could have answered some of the problems which had developed over the years with respect to the performance of the Foreign Investment Review Agency. They would have been used to establish constructive self-interest for Canadians.
I said at the beginning that I am pleased that the Government has at least indicated that it wishes to keep the basic premises in the Foreign Investment Review Agency, with some changes. To Members on this side of the House, I suppose small news is good news. In essence, at the heart of the Investment Canada Bill are some extremely good features. What might happen during this debate is that the Government might listen to some of the proposals made here constructively by Members of the Opposition and incorporate them into the new Bill.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Stevens that Bill C-15, an Act respecting investment in Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Regional Development; and on the amendment of Mr. Gray (Windsor West) (p. 1302).

Mr. Speaker, the debate being resumed today is on the amendment proposed by one of my colleagues to have Parliament postpone consideration of Bill C-15, an Act respecting investment in Canada, for a period of six months.
As a Member of this House and as a Canadian citizen who has worked for some time in other areas, including the private sector, I am very concerned about our country's economic future, the future of our children and the future of our workers, the future of the young and not so young. I want our colleagues on the Government side to understand the reasons for the position we have taken in this very important debate and the reason why we are asking for a six-month hoist.
Bill C-15 does not deal with the fundamental problems of the Canadian economy. Furthermore, the fifty or so clauses the Bill contains do not reflect the Bill's title, the "Investment Canada Act". In addition, as far as Bill C-15 is concerned, the premise that foreign investment is to be seen as a stimulus for creating additional economic wealth is ambiguous and uncertain to say the least. A number of statements by American and other foreign businessmen have confirmed this.
On the Government side they keep saying and there is some truth in this and I agree more or less with some of the things that have been said that economic recovery and job creation depends partly on the private sector's confidence in the economy and on increased investment by the private sector. To this I would like to add, for your consideration, that confidence cannot be generated unless the economic agents who make the decisions, that is, investors, managers, workers and consumers, are all aware of the rules of the game. Today, this applies both to Canadian citizens and to prospective foreign investors.
To ensure that everyone knows the rules, the Government must specify its policy on industries like the petrochemical industry, a very important one in the Montreal region where most of my riding is located, and also on the aerospace industry, which employs hundreds of thousands of people at Canadair in Ville-Saint-Laurent. The Government must also be specific about its policies on transportation facilities.
I am thinking, for instance, of the cuts at VIA Rail and the decision to scrap construction of a modern maintenance centre in Montreal that would have created about 3,000 jobs. This may mean that many workers currently employed by VIA Rail or the CN will be laid off, depending on what the Government decides to do.
There is also the telecommunications industry and the important textile sector. Can we consider allowing foreign investment in Canada in one of those sectors without knowing what specific policy the Conservative Government intends to formulate?
Another major industry in this country, especially in Quebec, is forestry. Can we consider letting foreign investors
January 24, 1985

set up business in Quebec, under the provisions of Bill C-15, without knowing the Canadian Government's policy on the forestry industry, a policy we have been promised for some time?
In the same vein, the Government will also have to make it clear what it intends to do about the changes it has promised in matters relating to financial institutions.
In addition, we are still waiting for clarification, and this could have a major impact on potential foreign investments, about the conditions which the Conservative Government will set before accepting to sell certain public corporations. We do not know what the policy of the Government is.
As long as these policies are not made clearer, we should not be surprised if European and American brokers and bankers tell us, as some of us who follow the statements of certain New York businessmen saw in the newspapers recently, that Bill C-15, as introduced by the Conservative Government, will do nothing to increase foreign investments in Canada. I can understand quite well what these businessmen mean. I can understand why an American bank president or broker could not, in all honesty, advise his customers that, if adopted, Bill C-15 would make it more beneficial for them to invest in Canada.
Moreover, Bill C-15 in itself does not help Canadian businessmen to invest in Canada. Yet, many reports have confirmed that Canadian companies are under-capitalized compared with American companies. This problem is especially serious for small businesses. However, Bill C-15 contains nothing which would give any hope to small businessmen that passage of this legislation will be of some benefit to them. On the contrary, the only other Bill under consideration in this House, which is the Bill to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act, will reduce the benefits provided to small businesses by lowering the ceiling of the guarantee which the Federal Government can provide for small businesses. In fact, representatives of small and independent businesses were quick to voice their disagreement about this initiative.
As I have already said, Canadian small businesses are under-capitalized. There is nothing in this Bill to solve this problem.
Some people will probably say that section 5(e) of Bill C-15 mentions the fact that the Minister will help to develop economic and industrial policies which will affect investments in Canada. However, neither this Bill nor any related proposal announced in the House by the Minister in his second reading speech have given any details about possible initiatives to increase investments by Canadians in Canada.
It is to allow the Government to take its responsibilities properly and to reflect before requesting passage of this Bill that Members on this side of the House have proposed a six-month hoist of Bill C-15.

I was referring to Section 56(l)(a)(B) of the Income Tax Act. The Department has advised that this Section permits the taxing of death benefits and it is this Section with which I would like to deal.
In my view, the death benefits which come from the Canada Pension Plan were not paid to the taxpayer in the two cases which I will cite. The benefits were paid to the estate of a young man who was killed in an accident in the first case, and in the second case the benefits were paid to the estate of a sister who died. Under the legislation, which has been in force over the last several years, the administration is now levying a tax against the parents of the young man and against the brother of the young lady. I want to deal with these cases from the viewpoint of the legislation.
I will quickly cite the two cases. A young man was killed in an accident. He was just over 20 years of age and had no estate. The parents, who could ill afford it, sacrificed and came up with enough money to bury their son. The Canada Pension Plan assisted with a grant of $1,500, which was payable as a death benefit to the young man who had paid into the plan. The funeral costs were well over $3,000, and the parents were very happy to receive this help. However, later they received a tax bill from the Department of National Revenue which taxed them on the $ 1,500 as if it had been income which went into their pockets. It did assist in the funeral expenses, but it was not income in any sense of the word.
In the second case, a young lady died. She had no parents. Her brother, out of the goodness of his heart, decided to pay the burial expenses. Again, a Canada Pension Plan payment was made to the estate. However, the brother later received a bill, as if the money had been paid to him.

speakeroldname: Mr. Geoff Scott (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Canada Pension Plan was introduced in 1966 provision was made to pay a benefit to the estate of a contributor on his death. The death benefit payable under the Canada Pension Plan is tied into the amount of pension to which the deceased individual would be entitled up to a maximum of 10 per cent of the yearly maximum pensionable earnings. In 1984 the maximum death benefit was $2,080. Any person who has contributed to the Canada Pension Plan for any three years qualifies for the death benefit.
As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, premiums paid under the Canada Pension Plan are deductible in computing income for tax purposes and, similar to other deductible amounts such as contributions to registered pension plans, registered retirement savings plans and unemployment insurance, the proceeds from the plan are included in computing income. This is a fundamental principle which facilitates compliance and ease of administration.
The Hon. Member has suggested that most people believe that the Canada Pension Plan death benefit is associated with funeral expenses. The amount of funeral costs is in many ways a reflection of personal choice-some spend much and others only a minimal amount. In view of the nature of such costs, it has always been considered as personal expenses for which no deduction from income for tax purposes has been allowed.
As I am sure the Hon. Member is aware, there are many individuals who are not eligible for death benefits under the Canada Pension Plan. To exempt Canada Pension Plan death benefits from tax under the premise that they serve to pay for funeral expenses would be unfair to those taxpayers who incur such costs but are not eligible for a death benefit under the Canada Pension Plan.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, the benefit received as a lump sum from the Canada Pension Plan and paid to the estate or to a beneficiary is a final payment based on a set formula. As
Adjournment Debate
indicated the contributions a taxpayer makes during his or her lifetime are fully deductible and distributions received are included in income. This is in keeping with well established principles of taxation and provides for equitable treatment to all beneficiaries; that is those in high marginal tax brackets pay proportionately more tax on the benefits received whereas those in low tax brackets pay little or no tax on receipt.

subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-BUDGETARY CUT-BACKS-EFFECT ON WINDSOR TELEVISION STATION. (B) REQUEST FOR CONSULTATIONS
CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-BUDGETARY CUT-BACKS-EFFECT ON WINDSOR TELEVISION STATION. (B) REQUEST FOR CONSULTATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in respect to a question which I directed to the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) some time ago. It is apparently more timely to now pursue the issue raised than it was then because, when I posed the question in respect to cuts which were threatened to CBET and the other CBC stations in Windsor, we were informed by the Minister that it was too early to deal with such issues on the basis that those cuts were merely rumours.
It turns out, Mr. Speaker, that the cuts at Windsor were even more vicious and more serious than had been anticipated. While between 8 per cent and 10 per cent of staff and funding were cut at CBC stations across the country because of budget cuts, Windsor experienced cuts in both in the order of 25 per cent to 30 per cent.
We in the City of Windsor consider it a very serious matter. As I pointed out at that time, geographically, Windsor is almost surrounded by the United States because it is on a peninsula in the middle of Michigan, Ohio, and New York, at the periphery of the Great Lakes. It is a community in which some 12 American television stations can be easily received. Indeed, Windsor has been described-as I am sure the Parliamentary Secretary recognizes-as an area in which there is the highest density of broadcast reception in the world, the bulk of that being American.
However, it is not only the overwhelming influence of the broadcasting media which affects Windsor. The Parliamentary Secretary will also know that Windsorites are as likely to read the Detroit Free Press for the Detroit news. As I pointed out this morning, we are Detroit Tiger fans, Red Wing fans and Piston fans, and so on. At times it is difficult not to consider ourselves American, and this kind of attitude is not helped by the fact that the rest of Canada sometimes regards us, indeed, as being American and appears sometimes to cede us to the United States. Therefore, the issue of CBET in Windsor is a very serious one.
To be specific, some 63 jobs were lost and about 25 per cent of its budget shaved. There is deep concern that Windsor have access not only to Canadian programming generally, but that CBET fulfil its significant cultural function in presenting an opportunity not only for emphasis on local news and happenings but, as has been pointed out by the local musicians union and others, a significant opportunity for the exhibition of performing talents in the City of Windsor and the surrounding areas. As a result of those cuts that role has very seriously

January 24, 1985
Adjournment Debate
been affected and we are now left only with our evening news broadcast. We have lost our weekend news and virtually all local programming.
There is another aspect of Canadian broadcasting in the Windsor area of which we should not lose sight. As I pointed out previously, Windsor is a significant window to the United States. Indeed, Channel 4 as well as Channel 7 have now assumed the role of broadcasting material from the Windsor area which reflects an interest on the part of Americans as to what goes on, not only in Canada but in the local Windsor area. CBET has a prospective audience of some eight million people on the other side of the river and that is not without significance in terms of communicating what Canada is all about to the United States.
In raising the question, I sought a meeting with the Minister of Communications, which request was not responded to either when the question was posed in the House or when I subsequently communicated with him by letter. We have since met with Mr. Juneau and heard that the financial cuts to CBC were not simply applied to Windsor, a fact that we recognized, but seriously affected other communities which are isolated in peculiar ways across this country. To deal with the peculiar Windsor problems would only mean some other location would suffer, because there would not be any serious attempt to shift funds from the big centres such as Toronto and Montreal. So it seems unlikely that any profit is to be gained by talking to Mr. Juneau.
The people of Windsor still seek a meeting with the Minister and I would ask that such a meeting be arranged. I ask the Parliamentary Secretary to advise the Minister of our interest and make every possible representation to ensure that we will have an opportunity to engage in that consultation. He can perhaps think about how those telefilm funds not presently being used may be given to CBC, as requested by other groups, and perhaps relieve the financial burden imposed on the CBC and open up a window to treat the situation in Windsor and other locations with respect to local production a little more leniently.

subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-BUDGETARY CUT-BACKS-EFFECT ON WINDSOR TELEVISION STATION. (B) REQUEST FOR CONSULTATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am more than pleased, now that I am on somewhat more familiar ground than in my previous intervention, to address the concerns of the Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy), from really two points of view. First of all, as a representative of the constituency of Hamilton-Wentworth I come from the same corner of the Province of Ontario as the Hon. Member. More importantly, I reported from the Parliamentary Press Gallery
to CBET Windsor for a number of years before getting into my current profession. So I am very sensitive to his concerns with respect to maintaining the regional programming mandate of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
With specific reference to the CBC's programming mandate and the over-all cuts from the corporation's budget, the Minster of Communications (Mr. Masse) has requested the CBC to attempt to make budgetary reductions primarily in administrative areas. In this regard, the Minister was pleased to note that the corporation has managed the reductions so as to protect programming as much as possible. The Minister made this request so that the reductions would minimize the negative impact on Canadian producers and artists whose development the corporation and Government wanted to encourage. The objective is to ensure that public resources now devoted to the support of artistic and journalistic expression are employed in the most effective manner possible, and that budgetary restrictions do not jeopardize the federal Government's investment in the cultural development of the nation.
Regarding consultations, the Minister specified that they take place with due regard for the respective responsibilities of the Minister of Communications and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and not infringe on their respective mandates. While some reduction was announced in radio and television network expenditures as part of the corporation's reductions, the CBC has promised to do its best to maintain the basic volume of network programming, particularly as it affects regional programming. As well, it must include the needs of smaller and more isolated locations and the interests of minority language groups.
As an aside, Mr. Speaker, of interest to the Hon. Member, CBET Windsor has a bigger news staff than its Montreal counterpart in the corporation.
The corporation has, since last June, been conducting internal reviews to assist in revenue reductions. A number of erroneous reports and remours concerning regional programming and services may have come from that process. Given the complexity of the task and the inevitable review of different options for the CBC, any decision attributed to the CBC would of course not be official until formally announced by the Corporation.
In conclusion, I suggest that it is not up to the Government to determine where those cuts should take place. It is up to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
